heroes.subtitle: Monte-Carlo witnessed courtside Jannik Sinner def. Carlos Alcaraz 7-6 (7-5), 6-3 in 2 hours and 15 minutes on a blustery Sunday on the Côte d'Azur, Jannik Sinner rewrote the record books, reclaimed the world No. 1 ranking, and delivered the defining clay-court performance of the early 2026 season.
heroes.excerpt: Monte-Carlo Country Club, April 5–12. In 2 hours and 15 minutes on a blustery Sunday on the Côte d'Azur, Jannik Sinner rewrote the record books, reclaimed the world No. 1 ranking, and delivered the defining clay-court performance of the early 2026 season.
heroes.author: Millie Sealana

body.content:
The 119th edition of the Rolex Monte-Carlo Masters — played on the ochre clay terraces of the Monte-Carlo Country Club in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, France— was the finest ATP Masters 1000 final of the young season. Jannik Sinner defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz 7–6(5), 6–3 in two hours and 15 minutes of high-altitude tennis under blustery Côte d'Azur conditions to claim his first clay-court Masters 1000 title and reclaim the world No. 1 ranking.

The match was their ninth career final and the opening act of what the ATP is now calling the Sinner–Alcaraz era of clay. Alcaraz broke first in the second set — a piece of athletic brilliance from deep behind the baseline — but Sinner's response was clinical. From 2–1 down he reeled off five straight games, serving out the match on his first match point. "I felt close on the return games," Sinner said in his on-court interview. "The change came at 2–1, and I just tried to stay there mentally. Having this trophy means a lot to me."
/story-media/h-apr26-1-b2-2c1ab5355e.webp
body.caption: Upload photo or video

body.content:
The statistics are extraordinary. With the Monte-Carlo title, Sinner became only the second man in the Open Era — alongside Novak Djokovic in 2015 — to win the first three ATP Masters 1000 events of a single season (Indian Wells, Miami, Monte-Carlo). He also joined Djokovic and Rafael Nadal as the only players to win four consecutive Masters 1000 titles, having won the Rolex Paris Masters in November 2025. His season record at Masters 1000 level stands at 22 consecutive match wins.

Sinner begins his 67th week as world No. 1 on Monday April 14 — moving one clear of Alcaraz, who had held the top spot for 66 weeks. Both players are now tied on eight ATP Masters 1000 titles apiece. Their head-to-head moves to 10–7 in Alcaraz's favour overall, but Sinner leads in finals 3–2. In the doubles final, Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz of Germany defeated Marcelo Arévalo and Mate Pavić 4–6, 6–2, [10–8] to claim the title.

body.content:
Every April, the world's finance ministers and central bankers gather in Washington for the Spring Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. They come to read the forecasts, compare notes and, usually, to talk about growth.

In 2026, they came to talk about war.

On 28 February, US and Israeli strikes on Iran opened a conflict that effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas. By the time the meetings opened on 13 April, the shock had travelled through tanker routes, energy prices, fertiliser markets and inflation expectations into almost every economy on earth.
/story-media/h-apr26-2-b2-1896ada64c.svg

THE FORECAST

The IMF's April World Economic Outlook carried a title that said everything: Global Economy in the Shadow of War.

Its reference forecast put global growth at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027, a downgrade from January. That forecast rested on an assumption the Fund was careful to spell out: a conflict of limited duration, intensity and scope, with disruption fading by the middle of the year, and energy prices around 19% higher in 2026.

The Fund also set out what happens without that assumption. In an adverse scenario, with energy prices staying higher for longer, global growth slows to 2.5% this year. In a severe scenario, with deeper damage to energy infrastructure in the region, it falls to about 2% in both 2026 and 2027.

The IMF compared the oil shortfall, even if the fighting had stopped in April, to the 1974 oil shock on an annual average basis.

ENERGY RETURNS TO THE CENTRE OF ECONOMIC RISK

Energy prices reach an economy through every door. Higher oil and gas costs raise the price of transport and production, eat into household budgets and feed through to food. For importing countries, they weaken the balance of payments and put pressure on currencies.

The IMF's reference forecast has global headline inflation at 4.4% in 2026, easing to 3.7% in 2027. In the adverse case it rises to 5.4%. In the severe case, the Fund's illustrative figures reach 5.8% this year and around 6% next.

The pain is not shared evenly. Energy exporters collect higher revenues while living with the volatility and the wider consequences of war. Importers face the bill directly. Lower-income countries, where food and fuel take a large share of household spending and governments have little room to cushion the blow, are the most exposed of all.

HORMUZ

The real decisions of the week were not being taken in Washington.

On 17 April, Iran announced that it would reopen the strait. Mohammed Al-Jadaan, Saudi Arabia's finance minister and chair of the IMF's steering committee, welcomed the news and warned against reading too much into it. "The hope is that we will see a serious, serious, credible de-escalation," he said. "But until that, I don't think insurance companies would respond."

His point was practical. Oil can be produced again. Tankers will only move when insurers are willing to cover them. And, he added, "it will take a bit of time for producing countries to ramp up in response." The ceasefire in place that week was due to expire within days.

GROWTH BEYOND THE WEST

The Fund's figures for China told their own story: growth of 5% in 2025, 4.4% projected for 2026, and 4% for 2027. The world's second-largest economy is slowing as it rebalances, and the energy shock arrived on top of a property downturn and weak domestic demand.

Emerging markets have shown real resilience to the shocks of recent years. The IMF's warning was that elevated debt and limited fiscal space mean that any support governments offer now has to be narrowly targeted.

TECHNOLOGY INVESTMENT AND THE PRODUCTIVITY QUESTION

Before the war, technology investment had been one of the main forces holding the global economy up. Artificial intelligence drove demand for chips, computing capacity and data centres, and companies poured money into software meant to make them more productive.

The IMF named a reassessment of AI as one of the main risks to its outlook: a fall in the profits investors expect from the technology, or in the margins companies can charge for it, even if productivity gains arrive. Such a reassessment, the Fund warned, could cut investment and trigger an abrupt correction in financial markets.

The optimistic case remains powerful. Stronger productivity could lift growth for years and help ageing economies carry their demographic weight. The cautious case is that the costs arrive now and the gains arrive later, unevenly, and perhaps smaller than hoped.

TRADE, DEBT AND THE COST OF FRAGMENTATION

Trade barriers and geopolitical tension were already weighing on business decisions before the first missile flew. Companies have been moving suppliers, rethinking factory locations and hedging against sudden changes in policy. Governments are reaching for tariffs, subsidies, export controls and industrial strategy.

Fragmentation has a price. Duplicating supply chains can reduce dependence on a single country, and it also takes more capital and raises costs. Resilience has a cost.

Public debt narrows the options further. Governments may need to support households, businesses or strategic industries, while high borrowing costs and heavy existing debts limit how much they can do. Fiscal credibility matters because investors are judging whether governments can finance themselves without stoking inflation or choking growth.

Defence spending was the other new line in the ledger. The IMF noted that higher military budgets can lift activity in the short term, while adding to inflation, straining public finances and crowding out social spending.
/story-media/h-apr26-2-b14-d20c368cd8.svg
body.caption: The Borrowers' Platform, launched 15 April 2026: Egypt in the chair, UNCTAD as secretariat, 30 countries at the table.

body.content:
THE BORROWERS' PLATFORM

The most concrete step of the week came from the countries that owe the money.

On 15 April, on the margins of the meetings, developing countries launched the Borrowers' Platform, a forum run by and for debtor nations, with Egypt as chair, Pakistan as vice-chair and UNCTAD as its secretariat. Representatives of 30 countries attended, including 16 finance ministers and central bank governors. António Guterres, the UN Secretary-General, called it a breakthrough, and Barbados's prime minister, Mia Mottley, spoke at the opening.

The numbers behind it are stark. Developing countries spend close to 10% of government revenue on interest to external creditors, and the least developed nearly a quarter. Fifty-four countries, home to 3.4 billion people, spend more on servicing debt than on health or education. Since 2020, many have borrowed at two to four times the cost faced by the United States.

The platform will not restructure anyone's debt. Its purpose is to share experience, build expertise and give borrowers a collective voice in a system long organised around creditors.

A NARROWER MARGIN FOR ERROR

Central banks face an unforgiving choice. Tighten too hard and they deepen the slowdown. Move too slowly and inflation expectations settle at a higher level, making the eventual cure more painful. Finance ministers must protect the most vulnerable households while keeping enough fiscal room for the next shock.

No country can manage this alone. Energy supply, trade routes, financial markets and the effects of war are tied together, and a policy decision in one capital ripples outward, hardest of all into economies with the least capacity to absorb it.

The IMF's message was adaptability with credibility: respond to new information without abandoning the frameworks that anchor expectations, and target support at those who need it most.

THE OUTLOOK

The April 2026 forecast did not describe a world economy in collapse. It described one still growing, with resilience that had become thinner, more uneven and more dependent on a ceasefire, an insurance market and the returns on a technology boom.

A single headline number hides the differences. The same shock lands very differently on an oil exporter, an industrial importer and a low-income country already spending more on interest than on schools.

The world economy kept moving in April 2026.

The margin for error had simply grown narrower.

body.content:
Artificial intelligence feels weightless. A question typed into a window, an answer a second later.

The weight is somewhere else. It sits in the plains of west Texas, in the desert outside Abu Dhabi, beside a fjord in Arctic Norway and in the palm-oil country of southern Malaysia. It is measured in chips, transformers, cooling towers and power lines, and in a number that only a few years ago belonged to national energy plans: the gigawatt.

In 2026, the world's largest technology companies will spend more on that physical machinery than the entire world invests in producing oil and gas. The question every investor, utility and government is now asking is simple.

What does it really cost?
/story-media/h-apr26-3-b2-0367b352e1.svg

APRIL'S NUMBERS

April 2026 made the scale impossible to ignore.

On 7 April, Anthropic's annualised revenue was reported to have passed $30 billion, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. OpenAI had passed $25 billion in annualised revenue in February. Two companies that barely existed as businesses five years ago were now earning at the pace of large industrial groups.

A fortnight later, at Google Cloud Next in Las Vegas, Google split its eighth-generation TPU into two chips for the first time. The TPU 8t, built for training, scales to 9,600 chips in a single superpod, with two petabytes of shared memory and 121 ExaFlops of compute, almost three times its predecessor. The TPU 8i, built for inference, carries three times the on-chip memory of the previous generation and is designed for the low-latency demands of AI agents.

Every one of those advances needs a building, a grid connection and a power contract. The revenue is real. So is the bill.
/story-media/h-apr26-3-b4-d5f9e4b2b4.svg

COMPUTE IS A CAPITAL BUSINESS

Training a frontier model takes vast clusters of specialised chips wired together for weeks or months. Inference, the work of answering each request once a model is trained, is a different kind of cost. It never stops. A product with millions of users has to respond quickly, reliably and around the clock.

That makes efficiency a competitive weapon. Model design, chip utilisation, memory bandwidth, network layout and the scheduling of workloads all change how much useful work a system delivers for each dollar of hardware and each kilowatt-hour of power. A system can be brilliant and still too expensive to serve at scale.

The supply chain is narrow. Advanced chips depend on a handful of designers, foundries, packaging plants and equipment makers. Data centre developers need land, grid connections, cooling and reliable electricity. A delay at any one link slows everything behind it.

THE CAPITAL BILL

The four largest American cloud and platform companies have set out the biggest capital programme in corporate history.

Amazon told investors in February that it expects to invest about $200 billion across the company in 2026, up from around $125 billion in 2025. Microsoft guided to about $190 billion for its 2026 fiscal year. Alphabet raised its 2026 range to $180–190 billion and warned that 2027 would be significantly higher. Meta raised its range to $125–145 billion, citing higher component prices and data centre costs.

Together, the four are heading for roughly $630–650 billion in 2026. The International Energy Agency puts the capital spending of the largest technology companies above $400 billion in 2025, rising by a further 75% in 2026 — more, it notes, than the world invests in oil and gas production.

WHAT A GIGAWATT COSTS

The industry now prices AI capacity by the gigawatt, roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor.

Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has put the cost of a one-gigawatt AI facility at $50 billion to $60 billion, with much of that going on chips, networking and computing systems before a single wall is built. Meta's Hyperion campus in Richland Parish, Louisiana, shows the shape of the bill. Meta confirmed in July 2026 that the site will grow to more than five gigawatts, with a footprint Mark Zuckerberg has described as nearly the size of Manhattan. Construction alone is put at about $50 billion. With chips, Bloomberg has estimated the total could approach $250 billion.

The shell and its power and cooling systems vary sharply by city. One 2026 industry benchmark put construction at about $8.2 million per megawatt in northern Virginia and $9.1 million in Texas, against $9.7 million in Stockholm, $10.3 million in Dublin, $11.8 million in Frankfurt, $12.4 million in Singapore, $14.2 million in Tokyo and $15.7 million in central London. Land, labour and, above all, the price of power decide where the money goes.

THE UNITED STATES: STARGATE AND THE RACE FOR POWER

America remains the centre of gravity. The IEA estimates that the United States accounts for the largest share of global data centre electricity use, and the country is where the biggest single projects are rising.

Stargate, the $500 billion venture led by OpenAI with Oracle and SoftBank, is the emblem. Its first campus, at Abilene in Texas, is planned at 1.2 gigawatts. By late April 2026 about 200 megawatts were running, with completion expected in the fourth quarter of the year. Six further sites — two more in Texas, and others in New Mexico, Wisconsin, Michigan and Ohio — bring planned capacity above nine gigawatts by 2029, most of it due in 2028.

Plans are not buildings. OpenAI has already dropped an expansion of Abilene to 2.1 gigawatts, and Lordstown in Ohio has moved to ban future data centres. Local opposition, grid queues and equipment shortages are now as much a part of the American story as capital.

ENERGY IS NO LONGER A FOOTNOTE

Data centres used about 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, according to the IEA, up 17% in a single year while global electricity demand grew 3%. Consumption by AI-focused data centres rose by around 50%. By 2030 the agency expects total data centre demand to reach about 950 terawatt-hours — roughly 3% of the world's electricity — with AI-focused facilities tripling their use.

The grid cannot always keep up. Gas turbine orders rose 70% in 2025, and the IEA expects 15 to 27 gigawatts of on-site gas generation to power data centres by 2030, most of it in the United States. Supply chains for turbines, transformers and memory have tightened, and the agency expects the shortage of high-bandwidth memory to last until the end of 2027.

The racks themselves are changing. AI server power density rose elevenfold between 2020 and 2025 and is set to rise another fourfold by 2027, when a single rack could draw as much power at its peak as 65 homes.

WATER AND HEAT

All that power becomes heat, and heat must go somewhere.

America's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that US data centres directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water for cooling in 2023, around 64 billion litres, and that the electricity they used accounted for roughly twelve times as much again. Google's single largest site, at Council Bluffs in Iowa, used about a billion gallons in 2024. Its air-cooled facility at Pflugerville in Texas used ten thousand.

Liquid cooling, heat reuse and siting in cooler climates now shape where the next generation of campuses is built. In dry regions, water has become as political as power.

EUROPE: AMBITION MEETS THE PRICE OF POWER

Europe wants sovereign computing. Its energy bill keeps getting in the way.

Brussels has set aside €20 billion for a network of AI gigafactories, each planned around more than 100,000 advanced processors, financed through the European Investment Bank to attract private money. Ireland shows what happens when a small grid hosts a large industry: data centres used 23% of all the country's electricity in 2025, up from 22% the year before, and more than all the urban homes in Ireland combined.

The economics are unforgiving. In April 2026, OpenAI put Stargate UK on hold indefinitely, citing the cost of energy and the regulatory environment. Days later, the campus at Narvik in Arctic Norway — 230 megawatts, run by Nscale with the Norwegian investor Aker, and once marketed as Europe's first Stargate — signed Microsoft instead, which will lease 30,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs there on top of a $6.2 billion commitment made in 2025. Cheap hydropower and cold air still win.

THE MIDDLE EAST: SOVEREIGN WEALTH AND A NEW KIND OF RISK

The Gulf has the capital, the land and the energy, and it is spending all three.

Stargate UAE, a one-gigawatt cluster built by G42 with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank, sits within a planned five-gigawatt UAE–US AI campus in Abu Dhabi. Its first 200 megawatts are due in 2026. In Saudi Arabia, the Public Investment Fund's AI company, Humain, is reported to be targeting around 6.6 gigawatts over the next decade, in a country whose total data centre load stood at about 410 megawatts across some 40 facilities in mid-2026. AWS has committed $5.3 billion to a new Saudi region.

Then came the war. In early March 2026, Iranian drones and missiles struck three Amazon Web Services data centres, two in the UAE and one in Bahrain, knocking them offline and disrupting banking, payments and delivery apps across the region. Analysts believe it was the first deliberate air strike on data centres in a conflict. A former US National Security Council official suggested Gulf facilities might now need missile defence. Physical security has joined power and chips as a line in the cost of AI.

ASIA: SCALE, SOVEREIGNTY AND THE JOHOR SQUEEZE

Asia's build-out is driven by two forces: scale in China and India, and sovereignty everywhere else.

In China, Alibaba pledged RMB 380 billion, about $52 billion, over the three years to 2028 for cloud and AI infrastructure, and its chief executive has told analysts the company is likely to overshoot. Domestic chips from Huawei and Alibaba's own designs are carrying more of the load as US export controls bite.

India has become the new battleground for American capital. In December 2025, Amazon committed more than $35 billion by 2030, Microsoft $17.5 billion between 2026 and 2029, and Google $15 billion for an AI hub at Visakhapatnam with AdaniConneX and Airtel — together $67.5 billion. South Korea secured more than 260,000 Nvidia GPUs at the APEC summit in Gyeongju, shared among the government, Samsung, SK, Hyundai and Naver.

Malaysia shows the limits. Johor, across the causeway from Singapore, now has about 1,110 megawatts of live capacity, third in Asia-Pacific after Tokyo and Singapore, with more than 8.5 gigawatts in the pipeline. Vacancy is under 1%. Rising power and water tariffs mean a 50-megawatt facility could face up to RM120 million a year in electricity costs alone.

WHO PAYS, AND WHO CAPTURES THE VALUE

The money flows in layers. Chipmakers sell the accelerators. Cloud providers and data centre developers build the halls. Utilities and gas producers supply the power. Model developers rent the capacity to train and serve their systems, and businesses decide whether the tools are worth the subscription.

Each layer carries a different risk. Chipmakers ride the capital cycle. Cloud providers take on huge upfront costs and the danger of empty halls. Model companies have to make every answer cheaper to serve than it is to sell. The IEA notes that the energy used per AI task is falling by at least tenfold a year — but demand is growing faster still.

The test is output. Spending on this scale is justified only by productivity that shows up in real businesses, in faster research and in new services people pay for. Capacity built against optimistic forecasts becomes a burden when demand or pricing falls short.

THE NEXT PHASE OF COMPETITION

AI is becoming a contest in systems engineering as much as in model building. The companies that run compute, power, cooling and deployment most efficiently may win even when rivals have comparable models. For governments, the same infrastructure is a strategic asset, which is why Seoul, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Brussels and New Delhi are all paying for capacity of their own.

Not every task needs the largest model. Smaller, specialised systems, efficient inference and careful choices about where workloads run can be the better business where they do the job. The market that emerges is likely to hold many architectures, not one.

THE CAPITAL DISCIPLINE TEST

The real cost of AI is no longer hidden in a software budget. It is written into national grids, Gulf security plans, European energy policy and the balance sheets of the world's largest companies.

Some of the capacity being built today will look visionary. Some of it will look like the fibre-optic glut of 2001. The difference will come down to discipline: where it is built, how it is powered, how efficiently it runs and whether the services on top of it earn their keep.

The race is no longer about the model.

It is about the stack beneath it, and the bill that comes with it.

articles.excerpt: The 90th Masters Tournament, Augusta National, April 9–12. Rory McIlroy defended his title, joining Jack Nicklaus, Nick Faldo and Tiger Woods as the only players to win back-to-back. He broke records and did it the hard way.
articles.author: James Whitfield

body.content:
The 90th Masters Tournament, played April 9–12 at Augusta National Golf Club in Augusta, Georgia, was not a procession. It was barely controlled chaos resolved by one of sport's most resilient performers.

Rory McIlroy entered the final round with a six-shot lead, the largest 54-hole advantage in Masters history. He did not make it look easy. A third-round 73 had already trimmed his lead. On Sunday, Cameron Young and Justin Rose surged. At one point McIlroy was three shots behind. Then came Amen Corner — specifically, the par-3 12th, Golden Bell. His approach flirted with Rae's Creek, kissed the greenside bunker's downslope, and finished six feet from the pin. He made the putt. He made birdie at 13. He never relinquished the lead again. His final round: 71 (1-under). Total: 276 (−12). Winner by one stroke over Scottie Scheffler (−11).
/story-media/a-apr26-1-b2-35fa519cb5.webp

McIlroy became only the fourth player in Masters history to win consecutive editions, joining Jack Nicklaus (1965–66), Nick Faldo (1989–90), and Tiger Woods (2001–02) — the last back-to-back champion until today. He is the first European to achieve the feat.

The 36-year-old Northern Irishman won his second green jacket and 12th major championship overall. The prize fund for 2026 was $22.5 million — the largest in Masters history — with McIlroy collecting $4.5 million. "I thought it was so difficult to win last year because of trying to win the Grand Slam," McIlroy said. "And then this year, I realized it's just really difficult to win the Masters." The question for 2027: can he become the first player in history to win three in a row?

articles.title: Time, Recalibrated
articles.excerpt: Sixty-six maisons. Seven days. One floor that reset the hierarchy.
articles.author: Millie Sealana
seoTags: Rolex Patek Philippe AP Geneva fair
Audemars Piguet return Watches and Wonders
IWC Big Pilot Perpetual Calendar Ceralume
Rolex GMT Master II Pepsi discontinued
articles.sources: Watches & Wonders Geneva official; Robb Report

body.content:
Palexpo hosted the most complete Watches & Wonders to date: Rolex, Patek Philippe, Vacheron Constantin, and Audemars Piguet sharing the same floor for the first time in the fair's history. AP's return after seven years was the structural shift. Everything else followed from it — a market no longer contracting, but reasserting position.

Every house launched something. But almost none of them launched a catalogue. Instead, each picked one object built to say everything at once — and the order they're considered in here isn't alphabetical. It's the order the room itself argued for, from the house that sets the cultural register down to the houses making the case for what comes next.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b2-3cbfa6e0ce.webp

CARTIER · TIMELESS CURATED LUXURY

The watch that happens to also be jewellery, and isn't shy about which one wins

Cartier's presentation was built as an environment rather than a showcase — immersive spaces in Geneva extending into Cartier Nocturne, where the boutique turned into an after-hours cultural setting once the lights came down.

The Crash Squelètte needed an entirely new movement just to exist — its case too asymmetrical for anything Cartier already had on the shelf. Limited to 150 pieces.

The Myst de Cartier pushed further: 112 hours of gem-setting, a 0.3mm gilded obsidian dial, an elastic strap with no clasp at all. Telling the time is, at best, the second thing it does.

Across the Roadster, Santos-Dumont, and Baignoire, the house kept its nerve: refine, don't reinvent. It's the harder discipline, and the one most houses lose the stomach for once they have something to prove.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b4-d975c88ec8.webp
body.citation: Photo courtesy of : Patek Philippe/ patekcom

body.content:
PATEK PHILIPPE · POETIC MECHANICS

Complication as a very expensive form of storytelling.

Where Cartier made its case in restraint, Patek made its case in narrative density.

The Ref. 6105G Celestial Sunrise/Sunset became Patek's first wristwatch to display sunrise and sunset times — six patents required to say something the sky has been saying for free, forever. $437,610.

The Ref. 5249R "Fox and the Crow" revived the automaton: press the pusher, the fox marks the hour, the crow drops the minute hand. CHF 320,000.

For the Nautilus's 50th, Patek resisted reinvention — three ultra-thin Calibre 240 editions, rotor engraved "50 1976–2026," from $75,019 to $112,529. The kind of anniversary only a house with nothing to prove can afford to keep this quiet.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b6-1bfc908365.webp

ROLEX · THE WEIGHT OF A CENTURY

Saying the most by changing the least.

If Patek's argument was narrative, Rolex's was leverage — the kind that comes from being the one house every other house is measured against.

The centenary of the Oyster case ran quietly through the collection — the kind of anniversary Rolex marks with a whisper, because it can afford to.

The watch worth queuing for was the Cosmograph Daytona Ref. 126502 — the first Daytona in Rolex's steel architecture to carry a Grand Feu enamel dial, housed in Rolesium and priced at $57,800 — a deliberate reminder that at this level, technique can outrank material.

More telling was what vanished. The GMT-Master II "Pepsi" left the catalogue without announcement — ending one of Rolex's most liquid modern sports references and immediately tightening an already starved secondary market.

Rolex rarely explains itself. Scarcity does it for them
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b8-e7c6916c01.webp

ZENITH · THE STONE THAT TELLS TIME

A watch that comes with its own alibi for being one-of-one.

Further down the floor, the argument got smaller and sharper.

The G.F.J. Calibre 135 set bloodstone into 18k gold, ensuring no two of the 161 pieces looked the same. A tantalum companion, limited to 20, made the same case in onyx — proof that uniqueness doesn't require a complication. Sometimes it just requires a mineral.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b10-df4a58852e.webp

JAEGER-LECOULTRE · THE IMPOSSIBLE MADE STILL

Engineering at the outer edge of what wristwatches can plausibly be.

The Master Hybris Inventiva Gyrotourbillon À Stratosphère rotates on three axes simultaneously — three titanium cages, three speeds, and among the most mechanically ambitious wristwatches currently being made. Twenty pieces. Price upon request — the kind of piece that exists less to be bought than to remind the room what's still possible.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b12-a55311d843.webp
body.citation: Photo courtesy of : IWC Schaffhausen / iwc.com

body.content:
IWC SCHAFFHAUSEN

One built for darkness. The other for orbit.

Where JLC made its case through mechanical extremity, IWC made its through application.

The Big Pilot Perpetual Calendar Ceralume® stores and emits light for over 24 hours — the kind of detail that means nothing on a spec sheet and everything at 2 a.m.

The Venturer Vertical Drive removed the crown entirely, built to be operated through a spacesuit glove and officially qualified for the Haven-1 commercial space station. €28,900. Most watches borrow the language of space. This one had to pass an actual qualification process to wear it.
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b14-45d01a50c2.webp

AUDEMARS PIGUET · THE RETURN

Seven years gone, and the room still remembered exactly who they were.

And then the room's centre of gravity reasserted itself.

The 150e Héritage became only the third ultra-complicated pocket watch AP has ever built — 47 functions, a Grande Sonnerie, minute repeater, and flying tourbillon inside platinum. Two platinum pieces. Eight in white gold. CHF 2.5 million.

On the wrist, the Neo Frame Jumping Hour and Royal Oak perpetual calendar made the quieter version of the same argument: history, run through a newer engine
/story-media/a-apr26-2-b16-318f0d669c.webp
body.caption: Featured image
body.citation: Photo courtesy of : Vacheron Constantin / vacheron-constantin.com

body.content:
VACHERON CONSTANTIN · QUIET DOMINANCE

The flex of having nothing left to add.

If AP's return was about scale, Vacheron's was the opposite proof — that authority doesn't require an announcement.

The Overseas Ultra-Thin Ref. 2500V/210P-H028 is the slimmest Overseas ever made — 7.35mm in platinum, salmon dial, 255 pieces, seven years of development.

Barely discussed before the doors opened. By the close of the week, the fair's quiet consensus — which is, for a house this disciplined, exactly the outcome it was built for

WHAT THIS WEEK ACTUALLY SHOWED

None of this was about volume. Sixty-six maisons exhibited; eight made the argument that mattered. Each chose one object, said one thing through it, and trusted the room to be sophisticated enough to hear it without a press release explaining the point.

That trust is the actual story of Geneva 2026 — and the reason this gathering will be read, in hindsight, less as a product cycle than as a recalibration of what these houses believe their most discerning collectors already understand.

POSTSCRIPT · MAY 16, 2026

The Royal Oak, translated for people who'd never set foot in a boutique.

Four weeks later, AP and Swatch released the Royal Pop — Royal Oak geometry in bioceramic, from $400, sold exclusively through Swatch.
The first time in 54 years AP licensed the design externally. A heritage house, briefly fluent in a different language — and confident enough in what it owns to know the difference between dilution and reach.

articles.excerpt: Art Dubai, 20th Anniversary Edition, Madinat Jumeirah, May 14–17. Free entry for the first time. Record attendance. Sixty percent of galleries from the region. The fair that built the Middle East art market came home.
articles.author: James Whitfield
seoTags: Safa Al Balushi Body as a Witness
Shumon Basar Before and After Everything
Busan Museum of Art Gulf collaboration
articles.sources: The National; Artsy; Emirates 24/7; Art in the Middle; Soigné Middle East; The Culture List

body.content:
Art Dubai's 20th edition opened May 14 for VIP preview and ran May 15–17 at Madinat Jumeirah — delayed from its usual March–April calendar by the Iran–Israel regional conflict that disrupted the broader Gulf cultural schedule. Rather than scale down quietly, the organising team redesigned the fair as a Special Edition and made entry free to the public for the first time in its 20-year history. The decision transformed the fair's character: record public attendance was confirmed at close.

The edition presented approximately 50 galleries — 60% from the region, spanning Abu Dhabi, Beirut, Jeddah, Ramallah, and Dubai — alongside international names including Galleria Continua and Pedro Cera. The guiding theme Things We Do Together integrated commercial galleries, artist commissions, and institutional collaborations under a single framework. Art Dubai co-founder and original director John Martin returned as a gallerist, two decades after helping establish the fair. "It's an incredibly well-loved fair," he said. "Much more like a family."
/story-media/a-apr26-3-b2-efb11a0f68.webp
body.caption: Upload photo or video

body.content:
Institutional highlights: Barjeel Art Foundation's Pulse — a 20-work exhibition of modern Arab art curated by Rimi Homsa, featuring Mahmoud Said, Samia Halaby, and Etel Adnan. Dubai Collection presented Made Forward, drawing from more than 20 private UAE collections. The Ministry of Culture's programme When the Familiar Becomes Unfamiliar spotlighted Emirati artists. Sharjah Art Foundation contributed live performances including Safa Al Balushi's Body as a Witness — a choreographic work on how the body carries memories of violence.

The 20th Global Art Forum, titled Before and After Everything, was commissioned by Shumon Basar. Institutional participation spanned more than 20 countries, with representatives from Zeitz MOCAA (Cape Town), Busan Museum of Art (South Korea), and MoMA (New York). In a fair year defined by the logistics of conflict — editors rerouting flights, retailers adjusting plans — Art Dubai's decision to remain open, to remain free, and to remain regional in its focus was its most consequential editorial statement in two decades. The region is no longer on the periphery. It is at the centre.

articles.title: Time as Luxury Infrastructure
articles.excerpt: Japan, the art of travelling slowly, and the value of an unhurried day
articles.author: Elena Voss
seoTags: Japan National Tourism Organization sakura forecast
articles.sources:
JNTO — Visitor arrivals to Japan, March 2026: https://asset.japan.travel/image/upload/v1776314432/pdf/Number_of_Visitor_arrivals_to_Japan_in_March_2026.pdf
JNTO — Visitor arrivals to Japan, April 2026: https://asset.japan.travel/image/upload/v1779271426/pdf/Number_of_visitor_arrivals_to_Japan_in_April_2026.pdf
Time Out — Japan Meteorological Corporation 2026 cherry blossom forecast: https://timeout.com/asia/news/the-2026-japan-cherry-blossom-forecast-is-out-heres-when-to-catch-sakura-in-full-bloom-010326
Aman Kyoto fact sheet: https://www.aman.com/sites/default/files/2023-11/Aman_Kyoto_Copy_Deck.pdf

body.content:
The first thing you notice in Japan is the pace.

A train arrives to the minute. A tea bowl is set down with care. A garden path bends out of sight and asks nothing of the person walking it.

In Kyoto, a whole day can be built around one temple, one seasonal meal and an afternoon spent watching the light move across moss and stone. The pleasure comes from having enough time to notice.
/story-media/a-apr26-4-b2-4c2f403e5b.webp

A COUNTRY IN DEMAND

Japan's popularity makes that kind of travel harder to arrange. The country now draws visitors on a scale few destinations match. The Japan National Tourism Organization counted 3,618,900 international arrivals in March 2026, up 3.5 per cent on the year before, and 3,692,200 in April. April's figure was 5.5 per cent lower than April 2025, yet it still meant more than 120,000 people arriving every day of the month. Between January and April, Japan welcomed 14,375,800 visitors.

Those numbers describe a country receiving millions of people every month. They also pose a practical question for anyone who wants to experience Japan with some intimacy: how do you find room in a place so many people have come to see?

The answer is time.

Not more of it, necessarily. Better use of it.

THE SEASON SETS THE PACE

Spring in Japan keeps a calendar of its own. Cherry blossom forecasts become part of travel planning, and the short window of full bloom can shape a whole itinerary. The bloom travels from south to north, and local conditions move the dates every year.

For 2026, the Japan Meteorological Corporation's first forecast, published in December, placed Tokyo's first Somei Yoshino blossoms on 19 March and full bloom on 26 March. Kyoto was expected to follow a few days later, with first bloom on 24 March and full bloom on 31 March.

Forecasts are guides. No one can promise the day a particular tree will be at its best: wind and rain can cut the display short, and a cool spell can stretch it. Travellers who give themselves several days in one place stand a far better chance of enjoying the season without turning each morning into a race across the city.

Kyoto rewards that flexibility. The city holds more than a thousand years of history in its temples, gardens and lanes. The most famous sites fill quickly in cherry blossom season, while smaller temples and quieter paths can offer a more personal encounter with the same landscape. Early starts help, and so does a guide who knows the corners most visitors walk past.

The same applies beyond spring. Autumn colour brings its own crowds; winter gives gardens and temple grounds a stiller atmosphere; summer brings heat, humidity and festivals with rhythms of their own. Each season asks for different choices. A journey planned around one spectacular moment can be rewarding. A journey with room to adapt is usually richer.

KYOTO, AWAY FROM THE RUSH

Aman Kyoto sits in the Takagamine district in the north of the city, inside a 32-hectare forest, a stone's throw from Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion. Designed by the late Kerry Hill, its 26 rooms, suites and pavilions take their language from the traditional ryokan — tatami floors, sliding doors, natural materials — and look out over the secret garden at the heart of the forest.

Its position changes the relationship with the city. Sixteen other UNESCO World Heritage sites lie within reach, yet the forest gives the stay its own rhythm. A walk through the grounds, tea, or an hour in the onsen fed by natural hot springs can fill an afternoon without a reservation anywhere else.

The appeal is in the detail. The garden changes with each season, from blossom and fresh maple to autumn colour and the muted tones of winter, and the rooms are made to frame it. The place encourages guests to stay long enough to notice changes in light, temperature and sound.

Aman Kyoto is one example of how Japanese hospitality makes time tangible. A room buys access to a place and its service. The more important decision belongs to the traveller: whether to leave enough space in the day to enjoy it.

THE CRAFT OF DOING LESS

Japan's culture of craft offers another way to understand time. A tea ceremony depends on preparation, attention and a sequence of gestures that cannot be hurried without changing the experience. The same respect for process runs through ceramics, woodwork, textiles, cooking and garden design.

Visitors usually meet the finished object first: a bowl, a lacquered box, a meal served on carefully chosen ware. Meeting the maker, or learning a little about the process, gives the object another dimension. The hours of work, the materials and the decisions behind it become visible.

That is why a good itinerary leaves room for workshops and encounters that need planning. A visit to a craft studio takes longer than a stop at a shop, but it gives a clearer sense of the place. A meal at a small counter restaurant may involve a long booking process and a fixed sitting, and it is often more memorable than a string of famous addresses.

The same is true of moving between cities. The rail network makes travel efficient, and speed tempts people to overplan. Adding another destination is easy on paper, but each move still costs time: packing, transfers, stations, checking in, settling. Fewer stops leave more time to understand each one.

A COUNTRY UNDER PRESSURE FROM ITS OWN APPEAL

The pressure is uneven. The best-known attractions and neighbourhoods carry concentrated crowds, while much of the country sees far fewer international visitors. Regional Japan offers a different perspective, particularly for travellers interested in food, craft, hot springs, coastline and rural tradition.

A longer stay in one region also brings more to local businesses. There is time to return to a restaurant, visit a market twice, or explore beyond the most photographed landmarks. Local guides and small inns benefit when a visit becomes a stay.

This is where time as luxury becomes practical. It shapes the length of a stay, the number of transfers, the choice of guide and the balance between booked experiences and open hours. The most thoughtful arrangements need planning well ahead, because access to a small studio, a specialist guide or a traditional inn is limited.

AUTUMN, AND THE JOURNEY STILL AHEAD

Japan's autumn calendar gives another reason to return. In Kyoto, the Jidai Matsuri is held each year on 22 October, a procession of some 2,000 people in historical dress tracing more than a thousand years of the city's past. The same night, the Kurama Fire Festival lights up the village of Kurama in the hills north of the city. Both draw large crowds, so rooms and transport need booking early.

Autumn colour arrives later, its timing set by altitude and weather. October can combine the festivals with the first turn of the leaves; November usually brings the strongest colour to Kyoto's gardens and temple grounds. Local forecasts are worth checking close to departure.

Japan can be travelled in many ways: by rail between the great cities, through rural inns, around a region's cooking, or with a focus on architecture and craft. The route matters. So does the time allowed for it to unfold.

The best journeys leave room for surprise — a garden found on foot, a conversation after a tasting, a meal that changes the plan for the evening.

Those moments never appear on an itinerary.

They need space to happen.

heroes.title: Milano Cortina 2026: The Nations, Champions and Defining Moments
heroes.subtitle: Winter Olympics · Italy · The performances and stories that shaped the Games

body.content:
Italy had spent years preparing to welcome the world to its mountains, cities and winter-sport venues. By the time the Olympic flame went out, the country had delivered its finest Winter Games, Norway had reasserted its command of the snow, and Brazil had made history in a sport long owned by the northern hemisphere.

The Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics, which closed on 22 February, brought 2,807 athletes from 93 nations to a competition spread across northern Italy. Milan supplied the urban stage; Cortina d'Ampezzo, Bormio, Livigno and the valleys supplied the terrain. The geography was part of the story. These were Games lived across a region rather than inside a single Olympic park.

The medal table told one story.

The athletes told the rest.
/assets/hero-olympics-BOZzxuCB.webp

NORWAY SET THE STANDARD

Norway finished first with 41 medals: 18 gold, 12 silver and 11 bronze. The United States placed second with 33 medals and 12 golds, a national record for a Winter Games that beat the ten won at Salt Lake City in 2002. The Netherlands finished third on golds, while Italy's ten golds placed it fourth in the official ranking despite 30 medals overall.

Norwegian dominance had a defining face in Johannes Høsflot Klæbo. His six cross-country golds made him the first athlete in any sport to win six at a single Winter Games, and took his career total to eleven — the first Winter Olympian to reach double figures. Only Michael Phelps has more Olympic golds. Klæbo's racing is built on judgement as much as strength: position, patience, and a finishing speed that arrives exactly when a race reaches its last climb.

For Norway, the result reflected the depth of a winter-sport culture that develops athletes across disciplines. Forty-one medals are not the work of one star. They are the output of a system that produces champions in endurance events and technical ones alike.

The United States combined strength across the programme with moments of personal redemption. The Netherlands again showed its extraordinary standing on the speed-skating oval, with ten golds among its 20 medals.

ITALY'S HOME GAMES BECAME A RECORD

Italy arrived carrying the expectations of a host. It left with 30 medals — ten gold, six silver and 14 bronze — beating the national Winter Olympic record of 20 set at Lillehammer in 1994, and with more golds than at any previous Winter Games. Italian athletes reached the podium in ten sports, well beyond the country's traditional strengths.

Few stories carried the emotion of a home Games like Francesca Lollobrigida's. She won the women's 3,000 metres on 7 February, her 35th birthday, and returned five days later to win the 5,000 metres, becoming the first Italian, man or woman, to win two individual Olympic speed-skating events.

The second victory asked for a different discipline. Over the longer distance she had to manage her pace and save enough for the final laps. She stopped the clock at 6:46.17, one tenth of a second ahead of the Netherlands' Merel Conijn, with Norway's Ragne Wiklund just behind in 6:46.34. After more than six minutes of racing, the margin was almost impossibly small.

Federica Brignone supplied another defining Italian performance, winning both the women's super-G and the giant slalom. Her two golds resonated in a sport where a single mistake can undo years of preparation, and they came in a career that had looked, not long before, as if it might be over.

Italy's successes reached beyond the established disciplines. In Livigno, Simone Deromedis won the men's ski cross with Federico Tomasoni second, an Italian one-two in freestyle skiing. On the oval, Davide Ghiotto, Andrea Giovannini and Michele Malfatti beat a heavily favoured United States team in the final of the men's team pursuit.

For the host country, the significance lay in the breadth of the achievement. The record was built across sports, generations and venues. The crowds had their individual heroes, but the larger accomplishment was a national team performing at a level it had never reached before.

A NEW GEOGRAPHY OF WINTER SPORT

One of the most consequential results came in the men's giant slalom. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen won gold for Brazil, the first Winter Olympic medal for any South American nation, and went one step further than a medal by winning outright. Switzerland's Marco Odermatt took silver and Loïc Meillard bronze.

The result redrew the familiar map of winter-sport power. Brazil is not an Alpine nation, and its Olympic identity has always been shaped by summer sports. Braathen's win showed that winter sport's reach can extend well beyond countries with deep snow and long ski seasons.

It also carried a personal dimension. Born in Oslo to a Norwegian father and a Brazilian mother, Braathen switched his sporting allegiance to Brazil. In a Games organised around flags and medal tables, his victory brought identity and belonging into sharp focus.

China's Eileen Gu was again a presence in freestyle skiing. She won silver in big air and slopestyle and gold in the halfpipe, six medals from six Olympic starts across two Games. Freestyle is judged in seconds — amplitude, rotation, execution, composure — and Gu has made that pressure look routine.

Switzerland finished with 23 medals: six gold, nine silver and eight bronze. Its Alpine tradition was central. Franjo von Allmen won the men's downhill and super-G, then added a third gold in the team combined with Tanguy Nef, while Meillard took the men's slalom. For a country whose sporting identity lives in the mountains, these victories carried familiar weight.

EXPERIENCE, AGE AND THE LONG ROAD TO GOLD

Some of the Games' most affecting moments came away from the favourites.

American bobsledder Elana Meyers Taylor won the women's monobob at 41, ahead of Germany's Laura Nolte and her compatriot Kaillie Humphries. She had five Olympic medals already — three silver and two bronze — but never gold. Her two young sons watched her win, and a sporting result became a family moment that reached far beyond the finish line.

The achievement challenged the idea that elite winter sport belongs only to the young. Bobsled demands explosive power, precision and nerve, but it also rewards experience: reading a track, controlling a run, managing pressure across several heats. Meyers Taylor's gold was a victory of accumulated knowledge as much as athletic ability.

The Games offered other reminders of how thin the line between triumph and disappointment can be. In the women's giant slalom, Sweden's Sara Hector and Norway's Thea Louise Stjernesund tied for silver to the hundredth, and no bronze was awarded. Behind every final ranking sits a much longer history of training, injury, selection and sacrifice, most of it invisible from the stands.

That tension is part of the Olympics' enduring appeal. The result is immediate. The journey is not.

THE MEDAL TABLE

The official final standings rank nations by gold medals, then silver, then bronze, which is why Italy's 30 medals sit below the Netherlands' 20.

Norway — 18 gold, 12 silver, 11 bronze (41)
United States — 12 gold, 12 silver, 9 bronze (33)
Netherlands — 10 gold, 7 silver, 3 bronze (20)
Italy — 10 gold, 6 silver, 14 bronze (30)
Germany — 8 gold, 10 silver, 8 bronze (26)
France — 8 gold, 9 silver, 6 bronze (23)
Sweden — 8 gold, 6 silver, 4 bronze (18)
Switzerland — 6 gold, 9 silver, 8 bronze (23)
Austria — 5 gold, 8 silver, 5 bronze (18)
Japan — 5 gold, 7 silver, 12 bronze (24)
Canada — 5 gold, 7 silver, 9 bronze (21)
China — 5 gold, 4 silver, 6 bronze (15)

WHAT MILANO CORTINA LEAVES BEHIND

The final standings will be remembered for Norway's supremacy, the United States' gold-medal record and Italy's extraordinary home performance. The Games also made room for achievements no national total can measure: Braathen opening a new chapter for South American winter sport, Lollobrigida's birthday gold and her second a few days later, Brignone mastering two Alpine disciplines, and Meyers Taylor reaching the summit after years of trying.

Those stories gave the competition its human scale. The medal table records who finished first, second and third. It cannot express what a victory means to the athlete who has waited years for it, to a country seeing itself represented in a new way, or to a home crowd watching a familiar name become Olympic history.

Italy set a new national benchmark. Norway confirmed its exceptional depth. Brazil found a place in Winter Olympic history. Across the mountains and arenas of northern Italy, Milano Cortina 2026 was a reminder that the Winter Games remain a contest of precision and endurance, and a stage on which the limits of the possible can still move.

heroes.title: Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels: How Rarity Shapes the New York Auction Market
heroes.subtitle: Jewellery · Collecting · New York · A blue diamond, a Boucheron wreath and the first jewels sold at the Breuer

body.content:
A jewel at auction has two lives.

One is the life everybody sees: the flash of a stone under the lights of a viewing room, the hush when the bidding starts. The other is written in paper. Gem reports, origin certificates, workshop archives, the names of every person who has owned it. In the New York saleroom, the price is decided where those two lives meet.

Sotheby's has staged its great New York jewellery sales, long known as Magnificent Jewels, for decades. In December 2025, it staged them somewhere new. The house had moved its New York headquarters into the Breuer building on Madison Avenue, the brutalist landmark that once housed the Whitney Museum, and the first jewels ever sold there went under the hammer in the second week of the month.
/assets/hero-sothebys-D7WSzZBJ.webp

A WEEK AT THE BREUER

The week opened on 8 December with a single-owner collection, "A Legacy of Elegance." Its 56 lots made nearly $14 million. The top lot was a Boucheron laurel wreath necklace from around 1888, which sold for $1.3 million.

The surprise was the twentieth century. Two bib necklaces by Suzanne Belperron, from 1954 and 1966, sold for $635,000 and $825,500, each more than double its high estimate. Pieces by JAR — Joel Arthur Rosenthal, whose work rarely appears in public — followed the same pattern: a rock crystal and sapphire butterfly brooch at $698,500, a wild rose brooch at $609,600, quatrefoil earrings at $698,500.

The next evening came the main event, now presented as High Jewelry. It made $30.1 million, with 94% of the lots sold.

THE TOP LOTS

A pear-shaped, 3.48-carat fancy intense blue diamond, sold unmounted, led the sale at $2.6 million. A Harry Winston ring set with a 22.85-carat emerald-cut D-colour diamond made $2 million. A Van Cleef & Arpels ring with a 26.55-carat cushion-cut Ceylon sapphire followed at $1.6 million.

1 — 3.48-carat fancy intense blue diamond, $2.6 million
2 — Harry Winston 22.85-carat D-colour diamond ring, $2 million
3 — Van Cleef & Arpels 26.55-carat Ceylon sapphire ring, $1.6 million
4 — 59-pearl necklace with a 3.78-carat fancy blue diamond clasp, $1.3 million
5 — Raymond Yard 5.43-carat Colombian emerald ring, $939,800

The story of the night was further down the list. A David Webb necklace and brooch sold for $508,000, almost seventeen times its high estimate.

WHEN RARITY DOES NOT SELL

Two days later, the week's quieter sale told the other half of the story.

The Fine Jewelry auction on 11 December made $11.8 million. Its lead lot, an unmounted 3.63-carat fancy vivid purple-pink diamond estimated at up to $1.5 million, failed to sell. Rare colour is the most prized quality in diamonds, and still a buyer will not pay any price for it. Clarity, proportion and the estimate itself all count.

Across the three sales, the week brought in about $56 million.

THE IMPORTANCE OF PROVENANCE

Provenance can change the meaning of a jewel as much as its price.

A stone with a documented history, a piece from a great house, or jewellery from a celebrated collection can draw bidders far beyond its material value. In December 2023, also in New York, Sotheby's sold five jewels from the collection of the comedian Red Skelton for $3.7 million against a high estimate of $2.2 million. His Burmese pink sapphire ring made $1.1 million, around seven times its estimate. The jewels of Mary Tyler Moore sold in the same week, every lot finding a buyer.

That history must be proved, not assumed. Catalogues separate confirmed fact from attribution, and serious bidders read the condition reports, gemmological certificates and terms of sale before they raise a paddle. At this level of the market, transparency is part of the product.

THE RECORDS

New York has set some of the great prices in jewellery.

In June 2023, Sotheby's sold the Estrela de Fura, a 55.22-carat ruby mined in Mozambique, for $34.8 million, the most ever paid for a ruby at auction. It beat the record of the Sunrise Ruby, which made $30.3 million in Geneva in 2015. In December the same year, a 133.03-carat fancy vivid yellow diamond sold for $5.5 million, the largest of its kind ever sold at auction.

Records like these set the benchmark. They also remind buyers that the very best stones are not interchangeable. There is only one of each.

A MARKET FOR EXCEPTIONAL OBJECTS

The phrase Magnificent Jewels covers a wide world: historic signed pieces, contemporary creations and important single stones. Natural coloured diamonds, exceptional white diamonds, sapphires, rubies and emeralds each have their own collectors and their own logic.

Colour, clarity, size and origin all shape the price. A Kashmir sapphire or a Burmese ruby carries a premium that a stone of equal size from elsewhere does not. Treatment matters too: an unheated stone is worth far more than a heated one. Signed jewels from Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Bulgari, Tiffany & Co. or Harry Winston add the value of design history, craftsmanship and the name on the box.

The auction puts all of that under pressure. Estimates set expectations, and bidding reveals what someone will actually pay on the night. Two collectors who want the same piece for different reasons can send it far above its estimate, as the David Webb did. A technically superb stone can be left without a buyer, as the pink diamond was.

Auction houses also stand between private collections and public attention. Pre-sale exhibitions let buyers examine the jewels in person. Catalogues supply the photographs, descriptions and documents. Online bidding has widened the room to the whole world, and with it the responsibility to get every detail of the information right.

CRAFT AND COLLECTING

A jewel is both a technical object and a personal one.

A diamond's brilliance depends on the relationship between cut, light and proportion. A setting must hold the stone securely while letting it be seen. Metalwork, engraving and the arrangement of stones turn a valuable material into a design you can recognise across a room.

Some collectors want the great names. Others want the great stones, whoever set them. A Belperron necklace and an unmounted blue diamond are both rare, for completely different reasons.

THE SEASON AHEAD

Sotheby's returns to New York with its spring High Jewelry sale in June 2026, 119 lots led by white diamonds of more than 15 and 23 carats.

The stones are small enough to sit in the palm of a hand. The evidence behind them — origin, maker, ownership and condition — weighs as much as their beauty.

In New York, that is what sets the price.

heroes.title: Milan Fashion Week Fall/Winter 2026: The New Creative Direction of Italian Luxury
heroes.subtitle: Fashion · Milan · 24 February – 2 March 2026 · Gucci, Fendi and Marni open new chapters

body.content:
Milan has always been the city where fashion becomes product. The ideas shown on its runways travel within weeks to the workshops, mills and tanneries of northern Italy, and from there to the world.

In February 2026, the city had more ideas to test than usual. Gucci, Fendi and Marni were all entering new creative chapters at once. Buyers were weighing a difficult luxury market. And the whole industry was asking the same question: can a change of designer change a house's fortunes?

The week arrived exactly halfway between the Milano Cortina Olympic Games and the Paralympics, and the city leaned into it. The official campaign borrowed mountain scenery, sports equipment and the five Olympic colours. Organisers expected the week to bring around €320 million into the city, against roughly €200 million for a typical edition.
/assets/hero-milan-fashion-DtX6Xf3R.webp

A WEEK IN NUMBERS

The official women's calendar ran from 24 February to 2 March and listed 162 appointments: 54 physical runway shows, eight digital shows, 73 presentations — five of them by appointment — and 27 events.

Behind those numbers sits the real strength of Milan. Its fashion system includes specialist manufacturers, leather and textile expertise, showrooms, buyers and a deep network of suppliers that can turn a sketch into a product at scale. A runway collection here is read not only as a creative statement but as an early signal of where a house is going.

GUCCI — DEMNA'S FIRST RUNWAY

The most anticipated show of the week took place on 27 February. Demna presented his first runway collection for Gucci, after introducing the house to his vision the previous September with a debut collection, "Gucci La Famiglia."

The designer known for the provocations of his decade at Balenciaga surprised the audience with restraint. His lineup offered sleek, body-focused basics and drew on the minimalism of the Tom Ford years, the era that made Gucci the most desired house of the 1990s.

The cast underlined the point. Kate Moss, Karlie Kloss and Elsa Hosk walked alongside newer faces and musicians Nettspend and Fakemink, a mix of eras and audiences that said as much about Demna's ambitions for Gucci as the clothes did.

A first runway sets a direction. It cannot, on its own, prove the direction will sell. But Demna's Gucci arrived sharper and more focused than many expected.

FENDI — LESS I, MORE US

Maria Grazia Chiuri's debut at Fendi, on 26 February, was a homecoming. She began her career at the Roman house in 1989, and returned after nine years leading women's collections at Dior.

Her show carried a message: "Meno Io, Più Noi" — less I, more us. It was a statement about community and craft, and about a house built by five sisters.

The Baguette, Fendi's most famous bag, was reworked with beading, embroidery and animal prints. Around it, Chiuri set out to reconnect Fendi's Roman identity and its mastery of fur and leather with a contemporary wardrobe. Her appointment also mattered beyond the clothes: one of very few women leading a house of this size.

MARNI — A NEW INDEPENDENCE

On the same day, Meryll Rogge made her debut at Marni.

The Belgian designer, who had shown her own label in Paris, brought a lighter, more personal sensibility. Her collection had a '90s feeling, with stripes, oversized dots and bubble hems, a cheerful eccentricity that felt true to Marni's spirit without copying its past.

PRADA — THE INTELLIGENCE OF DRESSING

Prada offered one of the week's clearest arguments about how clothes are lived in.

Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons built the collection around layering, which the house called "a reflection of the multifaceted realities of women and the complexities of life." Fifteen models each walked four times, their outfits changing with each pass, layers added, removed and rearranged, as a wardrobe changes through a day.

Bella Hadid made her first appearance for the house.

The idea had a practical edge. At a moment when luxury customers are thinking hard about price and cost per wear, a collection that makes fewer pieces work in more ways is a persuasive proposition. Prada's point was not minimalism for its own sake. It was that complexity comes from how clothes are worn together.

BOTTEGA VENETA — THE CITY'S WARDROBE

Louise Trotter showed Bottega Veneta at Palazzo San Fedele, and her subject was Milan itself.

She set the hard, brutalist exteriors of the city's architecture against a softer, more seductive interior, and treated craft as the house's technology. Curved-shoulder shift dresses with belt straps, angular leather trench coats, loosely folded wrap skirts and long tunics with soft creases led to a burgundy lounging suit and a clipped-fur vest dress. The finale returned to the fibreglass pieces of her debut, sculptural and strange.

A MORE EXPRESSIVE SEASON

Across the week, designers were less inclined to retreat into caution. At Jil Sander, Simone Bellotti staged an intimate show in a conversation pit, with a soundtrack that included a reading by Kim Gordon. Silvana Armani and Leo Dell'Orco presented their first collection for Emporio Armani, combining men's and women's lines. Maximilian Davis paired a sailor neckline with a red leather power suit at Ferragamo. Max Mara showed sumptuous wool coats and cropped shearling, and Loro Piana's cashmere-blend denim stopped buyers in their tracks.

Madonna made a surprise appearance in the front row at Dolce & Gabbana.

A WEEK WITHOUT GIORGIO ARMANI

One absence hung over the calendar. Giorgio Armani died in September 2025, at the age of 91, and this was the first women's week in Milan without him. For half a century he had defined what Milanese elegance meant: soft tailoring, quiet colour, clothes that let the wearer lead. The collection from Silvana Armani and Leo Dell'Orco, who worked beside him for decades, was watched as closely for what it preserved as for what it changed.

THE OPENING STATEMENTS

The week's defining story was renewal. Gucci, Fendi and Marni presented new leadership. Prada examined how clothes change through wear. Bottega Veneta explored the relationship between the city and the wardrobe. There was no single trend, only a set of distinct answers to the same challenge: how to make Italian luxury feel essential again.

The commercial environment remains difficult, and a new designer can renew attention but not guarantee demand. The real test comes later, in the stores, with the customers, over the seasons ahead.

For now, Milan had made its opening statements.

The clothes will do the rest.

articles.author: Millie Sealana

body.content: There are nights when sport transcends the scoreboard — when what unfolds on a field of play becomes something closer to a statement of intent that echoes well beyond the final whistle. Super Bowl LX, played on a cool California evening at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, was precisely that kind of night. The Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots 29–13, claiming their second Vince Lombardi Trophy — and doing so in a manner that left no room for debate, no space for a comeback narrative, and no ambiguity about who was the superior team.

body.content:
FINAL SCORE

Seattle Seahawks  29  —  New England Patriots  13

MVP: Kenneth Walker III — 27 carries • 135 rushing yards • 2 receptions • 26 receiving yards



THE BAY COMES ALIVE
Long before a single snap was played at Levi’s Stadium, the San Francisco Bay Area had already crowned itself the unofficial capital of American sport. For the better part of a week, the region transformed — its streets, landmarks and cultural institutions absorbed into one extended celebration that felt less like a preamble and more like the main event itself.
Super Bowl Opening Night on Monday, February 2 set the tone. At the San Jose Convention Center, both the Seahawks and the Patriots made their only public appearances before the game — players and coaches taking the stage before roaring fans in what the NFL billed as the official kickoff to Super Bowl week. From that moment, the Bay simply did not stop.

The Moscone Center in San Francisco became the beating heart of the week’s festivities, hosting the Super Bowl Experience from Tuesday through Saturday — an immersive, family-friendly celebration featuring interactive games, NFL legends for autographs, and displays of every Lombardi Trophy and Super Bowl ring in history. The 2026 Pro Bowl Games, recast as a flag football showcase, also moved to Moscone South on Tuesday, bringing all-stars from both conferences to the heart of the city. Thursday evening saw the Palace of Fine Arts host NFL Honors — the league’s annual awards ceremony — while the Bill Graham Civic Auditorium rocked to Benson Boone. Friday night offered a choice of spectacles: Sting headlined On Location’s Studio 60 concert series at the Palace of Fine Arts, while Luke Combs and Teddy Swims took over Chase Center, and Post Malone headlined a Bud Light show at Fort Mason. The Ferry Building, draped in a ‘60 Years of Super Bowl’ interactive projection from Thursday through Saturday, glowed as a nightly reminder of just how much the Super Bowl and football meant to 

By the time Sunday arrived, the entire Bay had been living Super Bowl LX for six days straight. Levi’s Stadium was merely where it ended.
/story-media/a2-b4-6d3c1ac71b.webp

RETURN TO THE BAY

Super Bowl LX marked the grand finale of the NFL 2025 season, arriving Sunday, February 8 the and California hosted its 14th Super Bowl — second only to Florida’s 17 — a lineage stretching back to Super Bowl I in 1967. The last time the Bay Area hosted, in 2016 for Super Bowl 50, the Broncos triumphed. A decade on, the setting was identical; only the cast had changed.

THE MATCHUP: A RIVALRY RENEWED

The Seattle Seahawks (NFC champions, 14–3) faced the New England Patriots in a coast-to-coast showdown that evoked memories of Super Bowl XLIX — that agonising 2015 goal-line defeat for Seattle. Eleven years on, the Seahawks left nothing to chance. New England arrived as underdogs, led by breakout young quarterback Drake Maye.

THE DARK SIDE ARRIVES

The story of Super Bowl LX belongs above all else to a defence. Seattle’s “Dark Side” unit — the NFL’s No. 1 defence under coordinator Mike Macdonald — dismantled Drake Maye from the opening drive to the final whistle. Six sacks. Three turnovers. Eight Patriots punts. New England’s 331 total yards were inflated by garbage-time drives with the game already out of reach; the competitive picture was far bleaker.
/story-media/a2-b6-ccf5c295c5.webp

CRITICAL GAME POINTS

First Half — Ground Game Takes Hold

Seattle opened with clinical efficiency — a Jason Myers 33-yard field goal on their first drive. Kenneth Walker III exploded in the second quarter with runs of 30 and 29 yards. New England punted on all five of their first-half possessions, unable to gain a single snap inside the Seattle 43-yard line. At the break: Seahawks 12, Patriots 0.

Third Quarter — The Turning Point

Linebacker Derick Hall’s strip sack forced the first turnover. A Drake Maye fumble five plays later led to a 16-yard A.J. Barner touchdown, pushing Seattle to 19–0.

Fourth Quarter — Hope, Then the Dagger

Mack Hollins’ 35-yard touchdown reception cut it to 19–7 with 12:27 remaining, briefly sparking hope. It was extinguished almost immediately: safety Julian Love intercepted Maye, and Devon Witherspoon’s strip sack saw Uchenna Nwosu scoop the loose ball and return it 45 yards for the game-sealing touchdown — 29–7. Jason Myers, meanwhile, broke the Super Bowl single-game field goals record with five — connecting from 33, 39, 41, 41 and 26 yards.
/story-media/a2-b8-8cd7ba2f46.webp

THE HALFTIME SHOW

The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show, headlined by Bad Bunny which highlighted the fusion of cultures and appreciation that defines American sports, music and culture.  Spectators were infused with guest appearances from Lady Gaga, Ricky Martin, and Los Pleneros de la Cresta, fused Latin heritage, global pop and live spectacle into one of the most talked-about halftime performances in the last decade.


THE WIDER LENS

This was the first postseason since 2014 without the Kansas City Chiefs — a notable absence that reshaped the championship conversation. For Seattle, a second Lombardi Trophy closes a circle that opened more than a decade ago. For Drake Maye and the Patriots, this is a beginning, not an ending.

But on the night, in the Bay, at Levi’s Stadium — in a city still vibrating from six days of celebration — there was only one team: the Seattle Seahawks, their Dark Side defence, and a running back from Michigan State who ran into history.
