articles.title: Rio Carnival 2026: Viradouro Crowns Its Drum Master
articles.excerpt: Music · Rio de Janeiro · A perfect score, a tie for second, and a night for Mestre Ciça
articles.author: Marcus Demallier

body.content:
You hear the Sapucaí before you see it.

Long before a samba school turns the corner into the Sambadrome, the bateria announces it: hundreds of drummers, surdos pounding like a heartbeat, tamborins cracking over the top, the whole avenue shaking with it. In Rio de Janeiro, Carnival is a competition decided by judges with scorecards. But it begins, and ends, with the drums.

In 2026, the drums won.

Unidos do Viradouro was crowned champion of Rio's Grupo Especial with a parade dedicated to its own mestre de bateria, Moacyr da Silva Pinto, known to the whole samba world as Mestre Ciça. The school scored a perfect 270 points, a ten from every judge in every category.
/assets/article-rio-carnival-DfaCuj-V.webp

THREE NIGHTS ON THE SAPUCAÍ

Twelve schools competed for the 2026 title. The parades began on the night of Sunday 15 February and ran across three nights, each school given 80 minutes to cross the Sambadrome with its floats, its costumed wings, its samba and its drums.

The Sambadrome itself is part of the spectacle: Oscar Niemeyer's long concrete avenue, flanked by stands and boxes, built in 1984 to give Carnival a permanent stage. For three nights it holds the most concentrated display of music, design and choreography anywhere on earth, and the city watches every minute.

Four schools paraded each night. Viradouro went third on the second night. The final night, Tuesday 17 February, brought Paraíso do Tuiuti, Unidos de Vila Isabel, Acadêmicos do Grande Rio and Acadêmicos do Salgueiro.

THE STORIES ON THE AVENUE

Every samba school arrives with an enredo, a theme it spends a year turning into music, costume and floats. In 2026, the themes ranged from a president to a forest healer.

The opening night set the tone. Acadêmicos de Niterói, newly promoted as champion of the Série Ouro, paraded first with a tribute to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, tracing his life from Garanhuns in Pernambuco to the presidency. Lula was on the avenue to see it.

Imperatriz Leopoldinense followed with "Camaleônico," a tribute to the singer Ney Matogrosso and half a century of reinvention. Portela told "O Mistério do Príncipe do Bará," a story of Afro-gaúcho faith and culture from Rio Grande do Sul, the state with Brazil's largest share of umbanda and candomblé followers.

Those themes showed how much a parade can hold. A singer's career, a spiritual tradition, a forgotten healer or a sitting president can all become a story told by thousands of people in motion.

Mangueira closed the night with Mestre Sacaca, the healer from Amapá known as the "Doutor da Floresta," a keeper of Afro-Indigenous knowledge in the Amazon. A parade, in the end, is a public argument about who deserves to be remembered.

PRA CIMA, CIÇA

The title of Viradouro's samba-enredo said everything: "Pra Cima, Ciça!" — up with Ciça.

His story runs through half a century of samba. He began as a passista, a samba dancer, in 1971, and was also a mestre-sala before finding his place with the drums. He passed through Unidos da Tijuca and São Carlos, the school now known as Estácio de Sá, before joining Viradouro in 1999.

He left in 2009 and returned around ten years later. Since then, the school has been transformed. Viradouro won the title in 2020 and again in 2024, and Ciça's bateria, the Furacão Vermelho e Branco — the Red and White Hurricane — was at the heart of both.

In 2026 the school turned the parade around him. Ciça rode on a float with his drummers, playing as they crossed the avenue, a tribute not only to one man but to every ritmista who has ever carried a drum down the Sapucaí.

ASH WEDNESDAY

The results are read out on Ash Wednesday at the Cidade do Samba, category by category, judge by judge, while thousands of supporters hang on every number. On 18 February 2026, it came down to tenths.

Viradouro finished with 270 points, a perfect score. Beija-Flor de Nilópolis, with its samba "Bembé," and Unidos de Vila Isabel both finished one tenth behind on 269.9. Beija-Flor took second place on the tiebreaker, Harmonia, leaving Vila Isabel third. Acadêmicos do Salgueiro was fourth with 269.7.

Viradouro also won the Estandarte de Ouro, the prize awarded by the newspaper O Globo to the best school of the Grupo Especial. It was the school's fourth championship, after 1997, 2020 and 2024.

At the bottom of the table, the margins were just as cruel. Acadêmicos de Niterói finished twelfth with 264.6 and was relegated to the Série Ouro for 2027.

THE FINAL STANDINGS

1 — Unidos do Viradouro, 270.0
2 — Beija-Flor de Nilópolis, 269.9
3 — Unidos de Vila Isabel, 269.9
4 — Acadêmicos do Salgueiro, 269.7
5 — Imperatriz Leopoldinense, 269.4
6 — Estação Primeira de Mangueira, 269.2
7 — Unidos da Tijuca, 268.7
8 — Acadêmicos do Grande Rio, 268.7
9 — Paraíso do Tuiuti, 268.5
10 — Portela, 267.9
11 — Mocidade Independente de Padre Miguel, 267.4
12 — Acadêmicos de Niterói, 264.6 (relegated)

Just six tenths separated first from sixth. Portela, the most decorated school in Carnival history, finished tenth.

The top six returned to the Sambadrome for the Champions' Parade on Saturday 21 February, Viradouro closing the night as champion.

THE CITY AS A STAGE

The Sambadrome is only part of Rio's Carnival. Across the city, the blocos — the street parties — fill neighbourhoods from morning until long after dark, some with a few hundred revellers, some with crowds that stretch for blocks. On the final day of the Grupo Especial parades alone, the city counted more than fifty official street parties, with dozens more still to come before the season closed on Sunday 22 February.

The scale of the operation is extraordinary. Nearly 2,000 municipal guards were deployed across the city, 950 of them around the Sambadrome. More than 5,500 cameras fed the city's operations centre. Medical posts at the Sambadrome treated 2,843 people over the parades, and Rio's cleaning crews removed more than 1,400 tonnes of waste over the pre-Carnival and Carnival period. The city remained on its heat protocol, Calor 3, through the final night.

There was protest too. More than 700 women marched on the Sapucaí against femicide, using Carnival's biggest stage to demand attention for violence against women.

THE WORK BEHIND THE SPECTACLE

A samba-school parade is not a concert. It is a production of thousands of performers that has to move as one. The samba-enredo, the song written for the year's theme, is its musical centre. The bateria drives it. Dancers, the flag-bearing couple, the costumed wings and the floats turn the theme into a moving story that must cross the avenue in a fixed time without breaking apart.

The work starts long before February. Costumes are sewn and floats built over months in the schools' workshops, many of them at the Cidade do Samba in the port district. The music is rehearsed week after week in each school's quadra. A parade can be spectacular and still lose the title if a wing falls out of step, a float stalls or the singing loses the rhythm.

It is also an economy. Carnival fills hotels, employs costume makers, carpenters, welders and musicians, and keeps a musical tradition alive whose influence reaches far beyond Rio. Yet for the people who parade, the school is something else: a neighbourhood, a family tradition and a form of memory. At the Sambadrome, Carnival is less a single party than a festival of competing artistic institutions, each carrying its own history onto the avenue.

WHY THE DRUMS MATTER

Every samba school is judged across nine criteria: the commissão de frente that opens the parade, the bateria, the mestre-sala and porta-bandeira couple, floats, harmony, costumes, enredo, evolution and the samba itself. In each criterion the lowest mark is discarded, and a perfect parade scores 270. A single tenth can decide a title, as Vila Isabel discovered.

But the bateria is the engine. It holds the tempo for thousands of performers over 80 minutes, and if it falters, the whole parade falters with it.

That is why Viradouro's theme resonated so deeply. A school that won its title by honouring its drum master was also honouring the thing that makes Carnival work: rhythm, discipline and the hours of rehearsal in the quadra that the audience never sees.

A NIGHT FOR CIÇA

Rio's Carnival is often described in superlatives, and most of them are deserved. But its heart is local: neighbourhood schools, built over decades, competing for pride as much as for a trophy.

In 2026 that heart belonged to one man and his drummers.

Pra cima, Ciça.

articles.title: Miami International Boat Show 2026: The Technology Changing Yacht Ownership
articles.excerpt: Yachting · Marine technology · Miami Beach, 11–15 February 2026 · At its 85th edition, the show made the case that the most interesting thing about a yacht is no longer its size.
articles.author: James Whitfield

body.content:
For the first time since 2018, the yachts came back to Collins Avenue.

Along Indian Creek, between 44th and 47th Streets, motor yachts of up to 125 feet lined the water in front of Miami Beach's hotels. It was the most visible sign of the biggest change to the Miami International Boat Show in eight years, and a fitting way to mark its 85th edition.

The show ran from 11 to 15 February 2026, over Presidents' Day weekend. It is the longest-running boat show in Florida and one of the largest in the world, owned by the National Marine Manufacturers Association and the International Yacht Brokers Association and produced by Informa Markets. Organisers expected more than 100,000 visitors, more than 1,000 exhibiting brands and more than 1,000 boats across its sites. Its economic impact on the region is put at close to $1 billion a year.

A NEW MAP OF THE SHOW

The 2026 show was organised around three destinations, linked by free shuttles, golf carts and rideshare.

The Miami Beach Convention Center and Pride Park were the hub: boats up to 49 feet, engines, electronics, marine accessories and retail, with the Progressive Experience offering hands-on activities and boater education. The Miami Beach Yacht Collection on Collins Avenue held the in-water displays, from 30-foot powerboats to 125-foot motor yachts.

Across Biscayne Bay at IGY Yacht Haven Grande Miami, SuperYacht Miami showed the largest vessels and the brokerage fleet, alongside a new destination for sailors. Sailor's Cove brought sailboats, catamarans and sailing equipment together for the first time, with on-site training from the Annapolis School of Seamanship.

"This year, we're unveiling a brand new show layout that makes it easier than ever before to explore all three locations," said Andrew Doole, president of US Boat Shows at Informa Markets.

THE YACHTS

Among the larger vessels were Miss Michelle, at 122 feet, making her show debut after her launch in 2025, along with the 111-foot Anmax and the 98-foot Gatsby. Around 20 superyachts were making their first appearance at the show, and the fleet was notably young, with an average age of just over three years, against more than nine the year before.

Builders on show ranged across the industry: Azimut, Ferretti, Sanlorenzo, Princess, Sunseeker, Riviera, Prestige, Absolute, Pardo, Mangusta, Viking, Tiara, Vanquish and Sunreef among them.

Sailors had their own premieres. Aquila Catamarans brought eight yachts, including two world debuts, the 50 Sail and the 45 Sport. Balance Catamarans unveiled the Balance 502.

THE YACHT AS AN INTEGRATED SYSTEM

For buyers, the hull is only the beginning. A modern yacht is a floating operating system: propulsion, navigation, communications, safety equipment, energy management, air conditioning, water treatment and the hotel services guests take for granted.

Those systems now talk to each other. Navigation displays, engine monitoring, onboard networks and remote diagnostics increasingly work as one, letting crews watch performance, plan maintenance and catch a small fault before it becomes a lost day at sea. On a larger yacht, generators, stabilisers and entertainment systems all compete for the same space and power. The owner notices a quieter cabin and a smoother passage. The engineer manages everything underneath.

THE INNOVATION AWARDS

The Miami Innovation Awards, judged by the NMMA and Boating Writers International, showed where the technology is heading.

The Alternative Propulsion award went to ePropulsion's Spirit 2, a portable electric outboard. In propulsion equipment, the judges named two winners: Dockmate's Dockmate Pro, a wireless remote that lets a skipper control engines and thrusters from anywhere on deck, and Avikus Control from Avikus, HD Hyundai's autonomous navigation company. Lowrance won the electronics category for ActiveTarget live sonar, and Mercury Marine took the outboard engine award for Boost, with an honourable mention for its Mercury Keyless System.

Among the boats, Azimut's Seadeck 7 and Hurricane's SunDeck 3200 shared the cruiser and motor yacht award. Regulator's 35 won among centre consoles, Chris-Craft's Launch 27 among bowriders, and Yamaha's CrossWave among personal watercraft.

The common thread was simple. Technology that makes boating easier, safer and less intimidating — docking, navigating, finding fish — is what the industry is betting on.

THE COMMERCIAL VALUE OF EFFICIENCY

Owning a yacht means managing fuel, maintenance, crew, insurance, marina fees and refits. Technology can make those costs clearer. It cannot make them disappear.

Efficient design starts with the hull, the weight and the way a boat will be used, then extends to everything installed on board. Hybrid and electric propulsion offer quiet manoeuvring and lower local emissions, and suit some boats and some owners well. On many larger yachts, diesel still delivers the range and sustained power that long passages demand. The best engineering matches the system to the owner's real cruising pattern rather than to a label.

The show's mix of boats and equipment makes those comparisons possible in one place. Visitors can weigh propulsion concepts, navigation systems, tenders and sailing gear side by side, along with the practical details that decide whether a boat suits coastal days, offshore passages or long stretches aboard.

The same applies to sustainability claims. A yacht's footprint depends on its materials, its speed, its energy use, its maintenance and its lifetime. Buyers are hearing more claims than ever, which makes independently verified data more valuable than ever.

MIAMI'S ROLE IN THE GLOBAL MARKET

Miami sits at the crossroads of the American boating market and the Caribbean, with Latin America a short flight away. That position makes its show a meeting point for every kind of buyer.

Some arrive looking for a first day boat for the family. Others are weighing a 100-foot yacht, a refit or a charter arrangement. A strong marketplace has to serve both without confusing the product or the level of support each requires. The new layout, with smaller boats in the convention centre, yachts on Collins Avenue and superyachts and sailing at Yacht Haven Grande, was designed to do exactly that.

PERFORMING AS PROMISED

The 85th Miami show demonstrated the scale of the industry. The bigger question is how the market will meet rising expectations around technology, operating costs and environmental performance.

Integration and smarter propulsion make yachts easier to run. They also make service networks, cybersecurity and reliable support far from shore more important than ever.

For an owner, the most valuable technology is the technology that works when it is needed.

Miami showed what is available. The real work begins when a buyer matches it to the boat, the itinerary and life on the water.

articles.title: Collin Morikawa Wins at Pebble Beach by One Shot
articles.excerpt: Golf · AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am · A 4-iron over the Pacific, and the end of a two-year wait
articles.author: James Whitfield

body.content:
There are few places in golf where the scenery makes the decisions for you. The 18th at Pebble Beach is one of them.

The Pacific runs the entire length of the hole on the left, a sea wall holding it back, the cypress trees bent by decades of wind. On Sunday afternoon at the 2026 AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am, Collin Morikawa stood in the middle of that fairway with 235 yards to go, the tournament tied, and the ocean between him and the flag.

He took a 4-iron, started the ball out over the sea wall, and let the wind bring it back.

It finished on the green. Two putts later he had a birdie, a one-shot victory at 22-under-par, and his first PGA Tour title in more than two years.
/assets/article-pebble-beach-Dwc7Vh_0.webp

A WILD, WINDY SUNDAY

The final round was the kind Pebble Beach produces when the wind gets up off Carmel Bay. Six different players held a share of the lead at some point in the afternoon. Akshay Bhatia, two shots clear overnight, slid back with a 72. Min Woo Lee finished birdie-birdie for a 65 that set the clubhouse target at 21-under. Sepp Straka joined him there.

Then came the charge nobody saw coming. Scottie Scheffler began the day eight shots behind. He made three eagles, shot 63, and finished with a 6-iron to 30 inches at the 18th for a birdie that briefly tied him for the lead. It was nearly the biggest final-round comeback in the tournament's history.

Morikawa held his ground through all of it. He holed a 30-footer for birdie at the 15th, hit a 6-iron to eight feet for another at the 16th, then gave one back at the par-three 17th after a tee shot drifted towards the ocean.

That left the 18th.

THE LONGEST WAIT

Before Morikawa could play his second, he had to wait — around 20 minutes — while Jacob Bridgeman, in the group ahead, played a shot from the beach that ended in the water.

Morikawa said afterwards that he walked to the ocean and back about ten times to pass the time.

Then the 4-iron, the wind, the green, and the birdie. His closing 67 completed rounds of 69, 68, 62 and 67, a total of 266. The 62 in the third round, the best score of the day, had put him in position. The last swing of the week sealed it.

THE END OF A DROUGHT

The win was Morikawa's seventh on the PGA Tour and his first since the Zozo Championship in Japan in October 2023 — 45 starts and 28 months without a victory for a player who won two majors before his 25th birthday.

His ball-striking has always been the foundation of his game, and Pebble Beach rewards exactly that: small greens, a coastline that turns every club choice into a calculation, and wind that punishes anything less than precise. He also had personal news to share. He and his wife are expecting their first child in the spring.

The victory was worth $3.6 million from a $20 million purse, along with 700 FedExCup points, and lifted him to No. 5 in the world.

THE LEADERBOARD

1 — Collin Morikawa, 266 (−22): 69, 68, 62, 67
T2 — Min Woo Lee, 267 (−21): 67, 65, 70, 65
T2 — Sepp Straka, 267 (−21): 66, 66, 67, 68
T4 — Scottie Scheffler, 268 (−20): 72, 66, 67, 63
T4 — Tommy Fleetwood, 268 (−20): 67, 68, 67, 66
T6 — Sam Burns, 269 (−19)
T6 — Akshay Bhatia, 269 (−19)
T8 — Nico Echavarria, Shane Lowry, Ryo Hisatsune, Hideki Matsuyama, Jacob Bridgeman and Jake Knapp, 270 (−18)

Lee and Straka each took home $1.76 million. Scheffler and Fleetwood earned $877,500 apiece.

THE EARLY ROUNDS

The scoring started early. Ryo Hisatsune opened with a 62 and Sam Burns with a 63, and for two days the leaderboard belonged to players who would later fade. Burns followed his 63 with a 72 in the third round. Hisatsune's 74 on Saturday undid his opening.

Akshay Bhatia was the steadiest of the early leaders. Rounds of 65 and 64 put him level with Hisatsune at the top after 36 holes, and a 68 on Saturday gave him a two-shot lead going into Sunday. It was a position built on precision, on a course where one loose iron into the wind can cost two shots.

Morikawa's week turned on Saturday. His 62 was the best round of the day, a reminder of how good his iron play can be when Pebble's small greens are holding, and it took him from the edge of contention into the final groups.

Sunday's wind changed everything. Bhatia's 72 left him three shots back. Morikawa's 67 was enough.

WHY PEBBLE BEACH STILL MATTERS

The tournament began in 1937 as Bing Crosby's Pro-Am at Rancho Santa Fe, a gathering of golfers and the singer's Hollywood friends that everyone called the Clambake. It moved to the Monterey Peninsula in 1947 and has been part of the fabric of American golf ever since. Mark O'Meara and Phil Mickelson share the record with five wins each.

The list of recent champions shows how much the event has changed. Nick Taylor won in 2020, Daniel Berger in 2021, Tom Hoge in 2022 and Justin Rose in 2023. In 2024 the tournament became one of the PGA Tour's Signature Events, with a smaller, stronger field and a much larger purse, and Wyndham Clark won a rain-shortened 54-hole edition. Rory McIlroy took the title in 2025 at 21-under.

The pro-am format still gives the week its character. Professionals share the opening rounds with partners from business, entertainment and sport, and the early days have the easy atmosphere of a celebration. But once the weekend arrives, the Signature Event field leaves no room for an average day. This year, five of the world's best finished within two shots of each other.

A CHAMPION AGAIN

For Pebble Beach, 2026 added another chapter to a tournament that has always blended elite golf with one of the most beautiful settings in the game.

For Morikawa, it was simpler.

Twenty-eight months, one long wait in the 18th fairway, one 4-iron over the Pacific.

A champion again.

heroes.title: Davos 2026: The World Economic Forum Confronts a Fragmenting World
heroes.subtitle: Global affairs · Technology · Capital · Davos-Klosters, Switzerland · 19–23 January 2026

body.content:
The World Economic Forum's 56th Annual Meeting convened in Davos from 19 to 23 January 2026 under the theme "A Spirit of Dialogue." The phrase was deliberately aspirational. The meeting took place amid geopolitical fragmentation, shifting trade relationships and rapid technological change, at a moment when the institutions that once helped organise global cooperation faced increasing strain.

Nearly 3,000 participants from more than 130 countries were expected, including 400 senior political leaders, close to 65 heads of state and government, nearly 850 chief executives and board chairs, and almost 100 leading technology companies and unicorns. The gathering brought governments, corporations, investors, researchers and civil society into the same Alpine town, where public sessions ran alongside private meetings and bilateral discussions.

Davos remains unusual because it places political authority and economic power in close proximity. A head of government, a central banker, a technology founder and an investor may approach the same issue from different perspectives, but they share a limited window in which to test ideas, negotiate priorities and assess risk.
/assets/hero-davos-wef-YCcb0w46.webp

FIVE QUESTIONS FOR A CHANGING ECONOMY

The Forum organised its 2026 programme around five challenges: cooperation in a contested world; unlocking new sources of growth; investing in people; deploying innovation responsibly; and building prosperity within planetary boundaries.

The first challenge was geopolitical. Trade restrictions, strategic competition and changing alliances have made supply chains and market access matters of national security as well as corporate efficiency. Companies must consider where they manufacture, where they obtain critical inputs and how exposed they are to policy changes. Governments, meanwhile, must balance domestic political pressure with the economic costs of fragmentation.

The second was growth. After years in which capital was cheap and technology valuations expanded rapidly, businesses were under pressure to show where investment produces durable returns. Artificial intelligence was central to that debate, but the discussion had moved beyond the novelty of generative tools. Investors were asking how AI would change productivity, what infrastructure it required and which businesses could capture the value.

The third challenge was people: skills, employment, education and the distribution of opportunity. Automation and AI create new capabilities, but their benefits depend on whether workers and institutions can adapt. Training, labour-market transitions and access to technology are economic questions as much as social ones.

AI MOVES FROM PROMISE TO INFRASTRUCTURE

Artificial intelligence was one of the defining themes of the meeting. The technology's rapid progress had created new opportunities in research, healthcare, manufacturing and business operations, but it also intensified debate over energy demand, data access, safety and concentration of power.

The economics of AI increasingly depend on physical infrastructure. Advanced chips, data centres, electricity supply, networking and cooling systems are essential to deploying models at scale. That creates a different investment landscape from the early consumer-facing phase of the AI boom. The winners will not necessarily be limited to the companies building the most visible applications; they may also include the suppliers and operators that make those applications possible.

The issue is particularly relevant for Europe, where policymakers are trying to encourage innovation while preserving competition, privacy and public trust. Building a competitive AI ecosystem requires research and capital, but also reliable energy, access to computing and rules that give businesses enough clarity to invest.

The same technologies raise questions about accountability. As AI becomes embedded in consequential decisions, governments and companies must decide how to test systems, establish responsibility and respond when automated outputs fail. "Responsible innovation" is not a separate concern from growth; it affects whether the technology earns the trust required for widespread adoption.

CAPITAL IN A MORE POLITICAL WORLD

Davos also brought the changing relationship between capital and government into view. Businesses increasingly operate in an environment where industrial policy, sanctions, subsidies, export controls and national-security rules influence investment decisions. Markets remain global, but the assumptions that once encouraged companies to optimise almost entirely for cost and efficiency have weakened.

For investors, the result is a more complicated assessment of risk. A factory's location, a supplier's country of origin or a company's dependence on a single market can change its prospects. For governments, the challenge is to strengthen strategic resilience without raising costs so far that growth and productivity suffer.

The World Economic Forum's role is to provide a place for those competing priorities to be discussed. It does not make binding policy, and its meetings cannot resolve structural disputes on their own. Its value lies in convening people who rarely share a room and creating opportunities for conversations that may continue long after the event.

That distinction matters. Davos is often judged by the prominence of its participants or the visibility of its announcements. Yet many of its most consequential discussions occur privately, where officials and business leaders can compare assumptions and explore possible cooperation without the pressure of a public declaration.

PROSPERITY AND THE PLANET

The fifth programme theme—prosperity within planetary boundaries—brought energy, climate and resource constraints into the economic conversation. The transition requires large amounts of capital, new infrastructure and changes in how industry produces and consumes energy. It also creates competition over critical minerals, grid capacity and the technologies that will determine future industrial advantage.

Energy security and decarbonisation are increasingly linked. Governments want reliable and affordable supply while reducing emissions; companies need power for factories and data centres while meeting climate commitments. These objectives can reinforce one another, but they also produce trade-offs that cannot be resolved by slogans.

The challenge for policymakers is to create conditions in which investment can move at the scale required: predictable rules, functioning markets, viable projects and infrastructure delivered on time. For companies, climate strategy is becoming more closely connected to operating costs, supply-chain resilience and long-term capital planning.

WHAT DAVOS CAN AND CANNOT DO

The 2026 meeting was notable for the scale of senior political participation and the range of issues competing for attention. Nearly 3,000 leaders were expected, with more than 200 sessions livestreamed to audiences beyond Davos. That public programme offered visibility into the debates, while private meetings provided space for more candid exchanges.

But a gathering of influential people is not the same as a mechanism for collective action. The value of the Annual Meeting depends on what participants do after they leave: whether discussions change investment decisions, whether governments cooperate on shared problems, and whether businesses translate broad commitments into measurable work.

Davos 2026 took place at a moment when dialogue was difficult and necessary. Globalisation was being reshaped by strategic competition, AI was changing the economics of work and infrastructure, and energy and climate constraints were affecting industrial decisions. The meeting could not remove those tensions. It could bring their consequences into a common conversation.

The lasting question was whether that conversation could produce cooperation in a world increasingly organised around competing interests. For a week in January, Davos provided the setting. The harder work belonged to the months that followed.

heroes.title: Snow Polo St. Moritz 2026: Standing Rock Claims the Cup
heroes.subtitle: Equestrian · 41st Snow Polo World Cup · A last-second goal on the frozen lake

body.content:
Polo on snow should not work.

The ball is too light for the surface, the footing changes with every hoofbeat, and the horses must accelerate, stop and turn on a frozen lake instead of a lawn. And yet for four decades, every January, St. Moritz has turned Lake St. Moritz into one of the most extraordinary sporting arenas in the world.

The 41st Snow Polo World Cup was played from 23 to 25 January 2026. Six teams arrived. Three days later, Standing Rock left with the trophy, beating FlexJet 6–4.5 in a final decided in its last seconds.
/assets/hero-snow-polo-BUgVgSlN.webp

SIX TEAMS ON A FROZEN LAKE

The field brought together FlexJet, MACKAGE, St. Moritz – Top of the World, Azerbaijan – Land of Fire, Standing Rock and Investec, with teams rated up to 16 goals.

Polo's handicap system explains the half goals on the scoreboard. Every player carries a rating, and when one team's combined rating is lower than its opponent's, it starts the match with a head start on the board. A score of 7–5.5 is not a misprint. It is the arithmetic of a sport designed to make uneven teams competitive.

Friday set the tone. FlexJet beat MACKAGE 7–5.5, St. Moritz – Top of the World edged Azerbaijan – Land of Fire 4–3.5, and Standing Rock beat Investec 6–4.

SATURDAY'S SURPRISES

The second day produced three more close matches and the first upset.

Investec beat MACKAGE 8–7.5 in the President's Cup. FlexJet edged St. Moritz – Top of the World 5–4 for the Waldorf Astoria Maldives Ithaafushi Trophy. And Azerbaijan – Land of Fire beat Standing Rock 5–4.5 in the U.S. Polo Assn. Cup.

For Standing Rock, it was a warning. The team arrived in St. Moritz in form, having recently won the Bendura Bank Snow Polo in Austria. Losing by half a goal on Saturday meant there was no margin left for Sunday.

THE FINAL

Standing Rock fielded a 16-goal side: captain Phillip Müller, England's Max Charlton (6), Argentina's Raúl Laplacette (6) and Ignacio González (4). FlexJet, rated at 15, lined up with captain Joaquín Castellvi, Pelayo Berazadi (5), Uruguay's Pelón Stirling (8) and Tito Gaudenzi (2).

That one-goal difference in ratings gave FlexJet a half-goal start, and they led after the first chukka, 1.5–1.

Standing Rock edged ahead, 3–2.5 after the second chukka and 4–3.5 after the third, but never by more than half a goal. Max Charlton was the driving force behind Standing Rock's recovery, pushing the team forward each time FlexJet threatened to pull away. FlexJet kept coming.

Then, with only seconds left, Raúl Laplacette broke clear and scored. Standing Rock 6, FlexJet 4.5.

In a tournament decided by half goals all weekend, the champions won it by a goal and a half, and the last of those goals came almost on the bell.

THE FINAL STANDINGS

Champions — Standing Rock: Phillip Müller, Max Charlton, Raúl Laplacette, Ignacio González
Runners-up — FlexJet: Joaquín Castellvi, Pelayo Berazadi, Pelón Stirling, Tito Gaudenzi
Third — Investec, who beat St. Moritz – Top of the World 5–4.5 for the MACKAGE Trophy
Casablanca Cup — MACKAGE beat Azerbaijan – Land of Fire 5–4

The umpires for the final were Esteban Ferrari and Tim Bown.

HOW SNOW CHANGES THE GAME

Snow polo asks for constant adaptation. The ball is larger than the one used on grass and coloured to stand out against the white. It bounces less predictably and runs differently across the surface, so players must adjust their timing on every strike.

The horses work harder still. Traction, acceleration and braking all behave differently on a prepared snow surface, and the riders have to manage their mounts' footing while keeping the pace and precision of a high-goal match. The condition of the pitch and the welfare of the horses are the first priorities of the organisers. Without them, there is no tournament.

The game itself does not change. A clean pass, the angle of a run, the ability to keep possession under pressure — they matter on ice exactly as they do in Palermo or at Guards.

FORTY-ONE YEARS ON THE LAKE

Reto Gaudenzi founded the tournament in 1985, and the idea of playing high-goal polo on a frozen alpine lake has since become one of the signatures of the St. Moritz winter. It remains the most important snow polo tournament in the world.

Part of its appeal is the setting. The pitch is laid out on the lake below the town, the Engadin peaks rise on every side, and the crowd watches from the edge of the field in the bright, thin air at 1,800 metres. Part of it is the social life that grows around the matches, the friends who return every year, the families who make a weekend of it.

But the 2026 edition was remembered for its polo. Six of the nine matches were decided by a single goal or less.

A WINTER OF EVENTS

The polo opens a remarkable run on the frozen lake. A week later, on 30 and 31 January, The I.C.E. St. Moritz brought classic and modern cars onto the same ice for its International Concours of Elegance, with a static preview on the Friday and the cars driven in front of the crowd on the Saturday.

February belongs to the horses again. White Turf, raced on the lake since 1907, runs on three Sundays, 8, 15 and 22 February, with flat races, trotting and skikjöring, in which skiers are towed by riderless thoroughbreds at up to 50 kilometres an hour.

Few towns in the world can turn the same frozen lake into a polo field, a concours lawn and a racecourse in the space of four weeks. St. Moritz does it every winter.

THE RESULT

Standing Rock lost on Saturday and won when it mattered.

FlexJet started the final ahead and never stopped pressing. Standing Rock answered with patience, Charlton's drive and Laplacette's speed in the final seconds.

The score was 6–4.5.

On the frozen lake, half a goal is a long way.

articles.title: The 98th Oscars: One Battle After Another Leads Hollywood's Big Night
articles.excerpt: Film · The 98th Academy Awards · Dolby Theatre, Hollywood · 15 March 2026
articles.author: Charlotte Thames

body.content:
Paul Thomas Anderson had waited a long time for this.

Eleven nominations across nearly three decades, from Boogie Nights to Phantom Thread, and not a single win. On 15 March 2026, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, the wait ended three times in one night. Anderson won Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay and, with his producers, Best Picture for One Battle After Another.

It was the film of the night, with six Oscars. But it was not the only story. Ryan Coogler's Sinners arrived with a record 16 nominations and left with four, including Best Actor for Michael B. Jordan. Norway, K-pop and a school in the Russian Urals all found their way to the stage.

Conan O'Brien hosted for the second year running.
/assets/article-oscars-DnNXu0Ts.webp

THE FILM THAT WON THE NIGHT

One Battle After Another took six of the evening's awards: Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, Supporting Actor for Sean Penn, Film Editing for Andy Jurgensen, and Casting for Cassandra Kulukundis.

That last one was history. Casting was presented as a competitive Oscar for the first time in 2026, almost a century after the Academy began, and Kulukundis became its first winner. Casting directors have long argued that an ensemble is built, not found. The Academy finally agreed.

Editing mattered just as much. Anderson's film moves across years and points of view, and its rhythm depends on how scenes and performances are cut together. Jurgensen, who has worked with Anderson since Licorice Pizza, gave the film its pulse.

Penn's award was his third, after Mystic River and Milk. Few actors have won more.

The spread of the wins told its own story. One Battle After Another was honoured for direction and scale, and also for the quieter work that holds a complex production together: the script, the cut, the ensemble. It won across the whole process of making a film.

SINNERS AND THE POWER OF CRAFT

If One Battle After Another won the night, Sinners won the room.

Coogler's film had broken the record for nominations before the ceremony began: 16, more than All About Eve, Titanic or La La Land. It finished with four Oscars. Jordan won Best Actor, Coogler won Best Original Screenplay, Ludwig Göransson won Best Original Score, and Autumn Durald Arkapaw won Best Cinematography.

Arkapaw's win was another first. No woman had ever won the cinematography Oscar before. In a category that shapes how an audience sees a film before a word is spoken — framing, movement, light and colour — her work on Sinners was recognised as the best of the year.

Jordan became the sixth Black actor to win Best Actor, following Sidney Poitier, Denzel Washington, Jamie Foxx, Forest Whitaker and Will Smith. His partnership with Coogler began with Fruitvale Station in 2013 and ran through Creed and Black Panther. Sinners was its fullest expression.

Cinematography and screenplay are separate crafts that depend on each other. Coogler built the story and its characters from nothing. Arkapaw made that world visible, setting its light, its colour and the way the camera moves through it. Together with Jordan's performance and Göransson's score, the four awards recognised a film made whole: writing, image, sound and the man at its centre.

The ceremony also gave the film a moment of its own: a performance inspired by its juke-joint sequence, with the ballerina Misty Copeland among the dancers.

THE ACTING AWARDS

All four acting prizes went to first-time or long-awaited winners.

Jessie Buckley won Best Actress for Hamnet, Chloé Zhao's adaptation of Maggie O'Farrell's novel about Shakespeare's family and the death of his son. She became the first Irish woman to win the award, a fitting crown on a career that has moved from musical theatre to some of the most demanding screen roles of the decade.

Amy Madigan won Best Supporting Actress for Weapons, Zach Cregger's horror film. Genre performances rarely win at the Oscars. Madigan's did, nearly forty years after her first nomination, for Twice in a Lifetime in 1986.

Penn and Jordan completed the four.

The acting categories are the most closely followed of the night because they put individual performances in direct competition. Yet no performance stands alone. The script, the direction, the edit and the chemistry between actors all shape what reaches the screen, and this year's winners each came from films built around them with unusual care.

INTERNATIONAL FILM AND ANIMATION

The International Feature Film award went to Sentimental Value, Joachim Trier's Norwegian family drama. The field was among the strongest in years: Brazil's The Secret Agent, France's It Was Just an Accident, Spain's Sirāt and Tunisia's The Voice of Hind Rajab.

KPop Demon Hunters, the animated musical that became a global phenomenon on streaming, won Best Animated Feature. Its song "Golden" won Best Original Song, the first K-pop song ever to do so.

The geography of the winners was the story. A Norwegian family drama, a Korean-American animated musical and a film smuggled out of Russia all took home Oscars on the same night, a reminder that the Academy's map of cinema now reaches far beyond Hollywood.

Best Documentary Feature went to Mr. Nobody Against Putin, filmed from inside a school in the small Russian town of Karabash by Pavel Talankin, the school's videographer, as the war in Ukraine reshaped what children were taught. Talankin filmed the patriotic assemblies and parades he was asked to record, then fled Russia with the footage, and the American director David Borenstein shaped it into the film.

THE CRAFT CATEGORIES

Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein swept three craft awards: Production Design, Costume Design, and Makeup and Hairstyling. Avatar: Fire and Ash won Visual Effects, and F1 won Sound.

The short-film categories brought a rare tie. The Live Action Short award was shared by The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva. The Documentary Short went to All the Empty Rooms, and the Animated Short to The Girl Who Cried Pearls.

THE WINNERS

Best Picture — One Battle After Another
Director — Paul Thomas Anderson, One Battle After Another
Actor — Michael B. Jordan, Sinners
Actress — Jessie Buckley, Hamnet
Supporting Actor — Sean Penn, One Battle After Another
Supporting Actress — Amy Madigan, Weapons
Original Screenplay — Ryan Coogler, Sinners
Adapted Screenplay — Paul Thomas Anderson, One Battle After Another
Cinematography — Autumn Durald Arkapaw, Sinners
Film Editing — Andy Jurgensen, One Battle After Another
Casting — Cassandra Kulukundis, One Battle After Another
Original Score — Ludwig Göransson, Sinners
Original Song — "Golden," KPop Demon Hunters
International Feature — Sentimental Value, Norway
Animated Feature — KPop Demon Hunters
Documentary Feature — Mr. Nobody Against Putin

THE NIGHT IN THE ROOM

O'Brien set the tone early. "Let us celebrate," he said, "not because all is well, but because we work and hope for better."

The In Memoriam segment carried unusual weight. Rob Reiner, Diane Keaton and Robert Redford were among those remembered, three figures who shaped American film for half a century. The room stood for them.

There was lightness too. The cast of Bridesmaids reunited on stage, fifteen years after the film, and the audience treated it like a homecoming.

HOW THE YEAR WILL BE REMEMBERED

Awards do not decide which films last. But they shape how the industry remembers a year.

The 98th Oscars will be remembered for Anderson's long-awaited triumph, for a record-breaking Sinners, for the first casting Oscar and the first woman to win for cinematography, and for a night when the Academy's map of cinema reached from Oslo to Seoul.

One battle after another.

This time, Anderson won.

articles.title: ART SG 2026: Southeast Asia's Leading Art Fair Expands Its Global Reach
articles.excerpt: The fourth edition of ART SG brought White Cube, Thaddaeus Ropac, and over 100 galleries to Singapore — alongside Ai Weiwei's monumental installation.
articles.author: Taylor Chen

body.content: The fourth edition of ART SG returned from January 23–25, continuing to set the pace as the leading international art fair in Southeast Asia. Visitors encountered presentations by global heavyweights including White Cube, Thaddaeus Ropac, neugerriemschneider, and Perrotin — alongside a strong contingent of Asian galleries.
/assets/article-art-sg-Dun7oFNQ.webp
body.caption: Featured image

body.content: The fair coincided with Singapore Art Week, which transformed the city-state into a concentrated hub of exhibitions, installations, and cultural programming. The most talked-about work was Ai Weiwei's monumental 60-metre inflatable raft — placed between diners at Capella Singapore — a provocative commentary on displacement.

ART SG's expanded programming included curated sections dedicated to emerging artists from the Asia-Pacific region and collector-led talks that drew private collectors from Hong Kong, Tokyo, Jakarta, and Sydney. Singapore is no longer an emerging art destination. It is one.

articles.title: Abu Dhabi Art: The Gulf's Expanding Cultural Map
articles.excerpt: Collectors, galleries and a growing cultural district on Saadiyat Island
articles.author: Elena Voss

body.content:
By late November, the art world had another reason to look towards Abu Dhabi. The 17th edition of Abu Dhabi Art brought 142 galleries from 34 countries to Manarat Al Saadiyat, 53 of them exhibiting at the fair for the first time.

The figures are a fair measure of its reach. The more interesting story sat around them: artists from the Gulf and well beyond, commissions that left the fair hall for the desert and the oasis, and a cultural district still taking shape across Saadiyat Island.

Held from 19 to 23 November 2025 and organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, the fair brought together modern and contemporary galleries, collectors, curators and artists. Its setting is part of its character. Manarat Al Saadiyat sits within the Saadiyat Cultural District, alongside Louvre Abu Dhabi, where museums, public art and new institutions are changing the way visitors meet the city.
/assets/article-abu-dhabi-art-BNvHBV5b.webp

A FAIR WITH A WIDER REACH

Abu Dhabi Art began in 2007 at Emirates Palace under the name ArtParis Abu Dhabi, and took its present name in 2009. Since then it has grown well beyond an annual sales event, with exhibitions, commissions, talks, performances and public programmes that run through much of the year.

The 2025 line-up mixed returning international names — Pace, Mennour, Richard Saltoun Gallery and Hanart TZ Gallery among them — with houses such as Almine Rech and Perrotin, and specialists in rare books, maps and antiques. Aldar Hall gathered galleries from the Gulf and the wider West Asia and North Africa region.

The curated sections gave the week its shape. A Nigeria Spotlight presented seven galleries under the Nigeria Everywhere initiative, in partnership with the country's ministry of art and culture. Modern Türkiye, curated by Doris Benhalegua Karako, brought works by artists including Fahrelnissa Zeid and Burhan Doğançay. A Gulf focus showed Khaleeji artists such as Hassan Sharif and Mohammed Kazem, and a Collectors' Salon curated by Roxane Zand rounded out the programme.

For collectors, the gathering offered a wide range of practice in one place. For galleries, it opened access to a market shaped by regional collectors, international visitors and the cultural investment under way across the UAE. As at every serious fair, much of the value lay in the conversations around the booths: artists' careers, institutional acquisitions, future exhibitions and work that deserves a wider audience.

ARTISTS IN THE LANDSCAPE

The most distinctive part of Abu Dhabi Art is the work presented away from the gallery booths. Its Beyond Emerging Artists programme commissions young artists to make new work, and in 2025 it was curated and mentored by the Syrian-born artist Issam Kourbaj.

Three artists responded to Al Ain, the oasis city and UNESCO World Heritage site east of the capital. Salmah Almansoori placed her work in Al Ain Oasis, reflecting on disappearing spaces and memory. Alla Abdunabi, who explores the afterlives of objects, worked at Al Jahili Fort. Maktoum Al Maktoum, who builds symbolic worlds around belief and the human psyche, took Jebel Hafit, the mountain that rises above the city.

The programme treated Al Ain as both a real place and a metaphor — a landscape where memory lives in earth, water and plant life. The works were shown at Aleph Hall during the fair, and the Al Ain commissions remain on view until 26 April 2026, which makes them one of the season's better reasons to drive inland.

That approach matters to the way Abu Dhabi is building its cultural identity. Investment in museums brings international collections and artists to the region, while local and regional artists keep shaping the conversation. The strongest programmes let those perspectives meet as equals.

SAADIYAT AS A CULTURAL DESTINATION

Manarat Al Saadiyat works as an exhibition venue and as a gateway to the wider district, where a visitor can build a day around museums, public spaces and the waterfront.

Louvre Abu Dhabi remains the defining presence. Stand beneath Jean Nouvel's dome at midday and the sun falls through it in thousands of small beams, a rain of light moving slowly across the stone and the water below. Its collection sets works from different periods and regions side by side, showing how objects, ideas and techniques have travelled between cultures.

The district rewards an unhurried visit: a morning at the museum, an afternoon at the fair, dinner on Saadiyat. Distances and timing matter during major events, and a planned route saves an afternoon spent moving between venues.

Abu Dhabi's cultural calendar extends well beyond the fair. Exhibitions and commissions through the year give reasons to come back, and for anyone interested in art, architecture and museums, the city now supports a much longer stay.

COLLECTING IN A CHANGING MARKET

The Gulf's art market has drawn growing international attention, supported by collectors, galleries, institutions and public investment. Abu Dhabi's approach pairs museums and cultural infrastructure with an annual fair that connects local activity to international galleries.

The distinction matters to collectors. A commercial fair offers a concentrated view of work for sale. An institutional programme shows how a city is building its cultural resources over time. In Abu Dhabi the two have grown up side by side.

Established international galleries bring recognition and market experience. Galleries from the region introduce artists less familiar to visitors from Europe, Asia or the United States. The most useful encounters happen where those worlds overlap, in conversations about provenance, technique, history and the direction of an artist's practice.

Headline numbers are a snapshot. The lasting measure comes afterwards: which artists reach new audiences, which galleries return, which works enter collections, and which relationships formed during the week continue.

A CITY WORTH RETURNING TO

The 2025 edition arrived during a period of significant cultural growth for the emirate. The fair brought the international market to Saadiyat Island, while its commissions carried the experience out into the landscape and cultural life of Abu Dhabi and Al Ain.

For the traveller, the most rewarding visit leaves room for both: the fair's concentrated view of contemporary galleries and collecting, and the museums and site-specific projects that explain the place in which the fair happens.

Abu Dhabi has invested in culture on a scale that is changing the city's identity. The next chapter will be written by the exhibitions its institutions present, the artists they support, the collectors who engage with them and the audiences who keep coming back. The fair was one week of that story.

Saadiyat Island is where it keeps being written.

articles.title: Australian Open 2026: Alcaraz Completes the Career Grand Slam
articles.excerpt: Tennis · Melbourne Park · Two finals, two breakthroughs, and a record that had stood since 1938
articles.author: James Whitfield

body.content:
The Australian Open has always been the tournament where the tennis year declares itself.

Players arrive from the off-season carrying new coaches, new fitness, new ideas, and Melbourne in high summer tests all of it at once: the heat on the outside courts, the night sessions under the roof of Rod Laver Arena, two weeks that can turn a promising January into a defining season.

In 2026, the final weekend delivered two breakthroughs. Elena Rybakina won her first Australian Open title, beating the world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka in three sets. A night later, Carlos Alcaraz beat Novak Djokovic to win his first title in Melbourne and complete the career Grand Slam, breaking a record that had belonged to Don Budge since 1938.
/assets/article-australian-open-D0C-WUge.webp

THE ROAD TO THE FINAL

Neither finalist arrived fresh.

Alcaraz came through a semifinal against Alexander Zverev that lasted five hours and 27 minutes. He led by two sets, watched the lead slip away, and found his way back to win the deciding set 7–5. Djokovic's semifinal was just as demanding. He beat the two-time defending champion Jannik Sinner in five sets, ending the Italian's 20-match winning streak at Melbourne Park in a match that finished in the early hours of Saturday morning.

So the final brought together a 22-year-old chasing the one major missing from his collection and a 38-year-old chasing a record 25th Grand Slam title. Djokovic had played ten Australian Open finals before this one. He had won all ten.

A FINAL THAT TURNED AFTER THE FIRST SET

For half an hour, history looked as if it would repeat.

Djokovic took the first set 6–2 in 33 minutes, his depth and timing pinning Alcaraz behind the baseline. Then the match turned. Alcaraz began to dictate with his forehand, pulled Djokovic wide, and forced the ten-time champion to defend instead of attack. He took the second set 6–2 and the third 6–3.

The fourth was the battle everyone expected. Djokovic dug in, saving six break points across the set and refusing to let the match drift away. But at the decisive moment, Alcaraz broke through, won two of the last three games, and closed it out 2–6, 6–2, 6–3, 7–5 in three hours and two minutes.

As he left the court, Alcaraz signed the camera lens: "Job finished. 4/4 Complete."

THE RECORD THAT FELL

At 22 years and 272 days, Alcaraz became the youngest man ever to complete the career Grand Slam. Don Budge had held the mark since the 1938 French Championships, when he completed the set at 22 years and 363 days.

Alcaraz is only the ninth man in history to win all four majors. The Melbourne title was his seventh Grand Slam, to go with two each at Roland Garros, Wimbledon and the US Open, won from just 20 major appearances.

"It means the world to me," he said. "A dream come true."

Djokovic, beaten in an Australian Open final for the first time, was generous in defeat. He called the achievement "historic, legendary." At 38, he had come within one match of a 25th major. The title went to Alcaraz, but the run to the final — through Sinner, in five sets — answered a question many had stopped asking: Djokovic can still beat the best players in the world on the biggest stage.

RYBAKINA'S CALM UNDER FIRE

The women's final was decided by nerve.

Rybakina beat Sabalenka 6–4, 4–6, 6–4 in two hours and 18 minutes to win her first Australian Open and the second major of her career, four years after her Wimbledon title in 2022. The match was as close as a three-set final can be. Each player won exactly 92 points.

Sabalenka, last year's finalist, levelled the match by taking the second set and then went 3–0 up in the third. That is usually where finals end. Instead Rybakina won five games in a row, held her nerve as Sabalenka fought back, and finished with her sixth ace.

"It's hard to find words now," she said, before turning to her opponent: "I just hope that we're going to play many more finals together."

The win followed her WTA Finals title at the end of 2025. Only one other woman in the past decade, Caroline Wozniacki, has won the WTA Finals and then the Australian Open a few months later. Rybakina's power has never been in doubt. In Melbourne, it was her composure that made the difference.

THE CHAMPIONS

Men's singles — Carlos Alcaraz def. Novak Djokovic, 2–6, 6–2, 6–3, 7–5
Women's singles — Elena Rybakina def. Aryna Sabalenka, 6–4, 4–6, 6–4
Men's doubles — Christian Harrison and Neal Skupski def. Jason Kubler and Marc Polmans, 7–6(4), 6–4
Women's doubles — Elise Mertens and Zhang Shuai def. Anna Danilina and Aleksandra Krunić, 7–6(4), 6–4
Mixed doubles — Olivia Gadecki and John Peers def. Kristina Mladenovic and Manuel Guinard, 4–6, 6–3, 10–8

The mixed final gave the home crowd its own celebration. Australians Olivia Gadecki and John Peers defended their title, the first team to win the Melbourne mixed doubles in consecutive years in 37 years.

A SUMMER FESTIVAL AT RECORD SCALE

The 2026 tournament was the biggest the Australian Open has ever staged. A record 1,368,043 people came through the gates over three weeks, up from 1,218,831 in 2025. Opening Week alone drew 217,999, close to double the year before, and for the first time the whole Melbourne Park precinct was open for a full 21 days.

Prize money reached a record A$111.5 million, with A$4.15 million to each singles champion. At home, Australians watched 108.3 million hours of coverage, up 22 per cent.

The numbers explain how far the tournament has grown beyond the match schedule. Food, music and family days fill the grounds from morning to midnight, and Melbourne treats the fortnight as its summer festival. But the crowds still come for the tennis, and this year the tennis gave them two finals worth remembering.

A NEW CHAPTER

Every Grand Slam writes a page of history. Melbourne in 2026 wrote two.

Rybakina came back from three games down in a final set against the best player in the world. Alcaraz lost the first set of his final to the greatest Australian Open champion of all and then took the next three, and with them a record nearly nine decades old.

The Happy Slam opened the tennis year with a new name on the trophy, and a reminder of how quickly the future arrives.

heroes.title: SailGP from Geneva to Cadiz
heroes.subtitle: Rolex Switzerland SailGP Grand Prix on Lake Geneva delivered a dramatic mix of tactics, light winds, and a breakthrough victory for Germany
heroes.author: Millie Sealana

body.content: Last week's Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix on Lake Geneva delivered a dramatic mix of tactics, light winds, and a breakthrough victory for Germany in its first-ever Final and first event win. Switzerland hosted SailGP for the first time on September 20–21, and the local crowd got more than a glimpse of world-class foiling — they witnessed a pivotal moment in SailGP's competitive evolution.
/story-media/h-sailgp-b2-3b8836c356.webp
body.caption: Featured image
body.citation: Photo credit: Millie Sealana, The Magorium

body.content:
SailGP's first inland stop, on Lac Léman, announced itself by contrast.  Having stood on the shores of San Francisco Bay in March with heavy breeze funneling through the Gate, and the F50s in full flight. Arriving at Lake Geneva felt like walking from a rock concert into a watchmaker's atelier. 

Lake Geneva introduced a distinctly different challenge to a circuit normally defined by coastal and open-sea venues with its Swiss thermal winds, terrain-driven shifts.  The rapidly moving pressure bands the fans visibly witnessed lakeside, created a race environment where stability disappeared.

The wind never gave the fleet what it needed. Coverage of the event noted breeze sitting well below the roughly 28 km/h the F50s require for consistent foiling flight.  This forced the boats to oscillate between foiling and displacement mode as pressure came and went across the course. Races were shortened to fit the broadcast window, and on Day Two the hulls stayed mostly in the water, with positions changing on every puff. The result was tight fleet compression, few clean overtaking lanes, and a heightened emphasis on starts and  positioning. The margins weren't about reading the wind . Every crew can. This weekend was about the cost of a wrong answer: off the foils, in the water, gone.
/story-media/h-sailgp-b4-0cad6f4948.webp

Geneva's lighter inland winds neutralized much of the sustained speed advantage typically held by the circuit's strongest teams — and the results showed it.

Spain, helmed by Diego Botín, arrived as the defending champions with two event wins already banked this season - back-to-back victories in San Francisco and New York. Botín, alongside Florian Trittel, forms a pairing that defines Spain's campaign: the duo are the reigning Olympic 49er gold medalists and World Sailors of the Year, arguably the most decorated active Olympic partnership in SailGP. But on the lake, nothing held long enough for rhythm to become distance. A win in Race 5 was their best moment of the weekend, and Spain finished fifth overall — never able to string continuity out of a fragmented light wind.

New Zealand fared worse. The usually dominant Black Foils endured a challenging weekend, slipping from the top of the season standings to third. The United States, disqualified from the first race for a barging foul, found the non-foiling conditions of day two more to their liking. Mubadala Brazil missed both fleet races on Sunday entirely after pre-race damage from a mark collision.

In marginal foiling conditions, the gap between the elite programs and the emerging mid-fleet narrowed dramatically. Execution errors — penalties, timing at the start line, split-second decisions in shifting pressure — carried far greater weight than boat speed. It reinforced a broader SailGP truth: being at the  wind's mercy.  This is the challenge that every team faces going into each race – especially on Lac Leman.
/story-media/h-sailgp-b6-d159cffe09.webp

By the Final, a light drizzle  had settled over the lake, and attention shifted to the home team.  Sébastien Schneiter — a Geneva native, three-time Olympian, and one of SailGP's younger helms — carried both the energy of a home crowd and the weight of a breakthrough opportunity on home waters.

The Swiss had earned their place. Fleet scores of 5-2-8-7-2 put them into the three-boat Final alongside Germany and Australia — their second event Final in four events, a mark of how sharply the team's trajectory has climbed this season. A month earlier in Sassnitz, they had stunned the fleet with a surprise Race 7 win. Geneva was not a fluke of local knowledge; it was a team on a climb reaching its home water at the right moment.

"It's good to be doing another final, and doing it at home is extra special," Schneiter said. "It shows the good character of the team, being able to deliver under pressure." 

For stretches of the weekend, Switzerland looked capable of delivering a historic home-water victory. But in a race defined by precision, the Final ended almost before it began: Switzerland were over early at the start and forced to take a pre-start penalty, immediately ceding position and clean air. In conditions that punished every interruption, there was no way back. Schneiter's team crossed third, some 46 seconds behind the winners .

If the result stung, the weekend didn't. "I think this home event will be remembered for the people that attended, the support we got, and the emotions we lived," Schneiter reflected afterward . From inside the Yacht Club de Genève, the whole theatre was legible: the grandstands filling along the quai, the spectator fleet holding station, the pressure bands crossing the lake like slow weather. Thousands had embraced a championship usually associated with harbors and coastlines.  In Geneva, lakeside, SailGP felt less like a travelling race series than a natural extension of Switzerland's culture of precision engineering and elite sport.
/story-media/h-sailgp-b8-9dc034807b.webp
body.caption: Australia and Switzerland in the Final, six minutes before Germany crossed the line.

body.content:
Erik Heil's German team delivered a disciplined Final — clean off the line, careful in transitions, selective in pursuit of pressure lanes. A perfect start put them in front at Mark 1, and though they briefly fell off their foils after the first rounding — opening the door for Tom Slingsby's Australia to close — the Germans got back up and flying to hold off the attack. They crossed at 15:33:03, nearly 20 seconds clear of Australia, with Switzerland 26 seconds further back.

one wave rolling over the club, the boxes, the quai, and out across the water. Everyone cheered. But only the stands could roar.

"It's part of the journey," Heil said. "We'll keep getting better. Sometimes it works out for us, sometimes it works out for someone else." 

The win underscored the growing parity across the fleet — Germany became the latest first-time winner in a season that has produced an unusually wide spread of them — and the increasingly unpredictable shape of the championship. Australia's second place was enough to reclaim the top of the season standings with 76 points, one clear of Great Britain, New Zealand third holding at 73 and Spain fourth with 70 .
/story-media/h-sailgp-b10-1479aef4d6.webp

As Germany celebrated and the podium ceremony wrapped, heavy Swiss rain swept across the venue — organizers had moved the racing forward one hour ahead of the approaching weather. For spectators, it became a fitting final image: a weekend defined by shifting winds, compressed margins, and a storm that seemed to close the story as dramatically as it unfolded.

Next stop - Cádiz, Spain, on October 4–5 — the season's penultimate stop before the Grand Final in Abu Dhabi.

heroes.title: CV Summit Zürich 2025: Digital Assets Move Toward Institutional Finance
heroes.subtitle: Finance · Blockchain · Digital assets · Kongresshaus Zürich · 23–24 September 2025
heroes.author: Millie Sealana

body.content:
Zürich is not a city that gets excited easily.

Its banks have watched currencies rise and fall, fortunes made and lost, and more than one technology promise to change everything. So when bankers, asset managers and blockchain builders filled the Kongresshaus on the shore of the lake for two days in September 2025, the question in the room was a sober one.

Is digital finance finally ready for the institutions?

CV Summit, now in its eleventh edition, brought more than 3,000 executives, investors, founders and policymakers to Zürich on 23 and 24 September. There were five stages, 190 speakers, more than 100 partners — from Franklin Templeton and Binance to Google, Microsoft and Palantir — and delegations from more than 80 banks and asset managers.
/assets/article-cv-summit-DYiJBnYb.webp

FROM CRYPTO MARKETS TO FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE

For years, digital assets were defined by token prices and speculative cycles. The conversation in Zürich had moved on. The talk was of settlement, custody, payments, tokenised funds and wealth management: the plumbing of finance rather than its casino.

A blockchain is, at heart, a shared ledger that records transactions and ownership. In financial services, that opens the door to faster settlement, programmable payments and the tokenisation of assets that have always lived in separate databases held by separate intermediaries.

Tokenisation changes how a right is recorded and transferred. It does not change the right itself. The legal claim, the custody arrangement and the regulatory obligation all remain. A ledger can prove that a transaction happened. It cannot prove that the issuer behind it is sound.

BANKERS IN THE ROOM WITH BUILDERS

"Our vision was to bring bankers into the same room as builders," said Mathias Ruch, founder and chief executive of CV VC, the Zug-based investor behind the summit.

In 2025, the bankers came with news. Luzerner Kantonalbank announced that it now accepts Bitcoin and Ether as collateral for loans, a step that would have been unthinkable for a Swiss cantonal bank a few years ago. The Swiss Bankers Association, UBS, PostFinance and Sygnum Bank presented a feasibility study on blockchain-based deposit tokens, including what they described as the first legally binding payment between institutions using bank deposits on a public blockchain.

Franklin Templeton's Sandy Kaul and Roger Bayston spoke on tokenised funds. Heinz Tännler, the finance director of the canton of Zug, spoke for the Swiss Blockchain Federation, and Ahmed Bin Sulayem of Dubai's DMCC brought the view from the Gulf. Philipp Rickenbacher, the former chief executive of Julius Baer and now chairman of CV VC, summed up the mood: "Innovation does not happen incrementally. It only happens in big steps."

THE SWISS ADVANTAGE

Switzerland did not become a digital-asset hub by accident.

Crypto Valley, the cluster that stretches across Zug, Zürich and into Liechtenstein, now counts 1,766 active blockchain companies. According to CV VC's 2026 ecosystem report, its 50 largest firms and projects — among them Ethereum, Solana, Cardano, Sygnum Bank and Copper — were worth a combined $467 billion, with ten valued above $1 billion. In 2025, Crypto Valley companies attracted 47% of all blockchain funding raised in Europe.

The law came early too. Switzerland's DLT Act came into force in 2021, giving legal recognition to ledger-based securities, protecting crypto assets held by a custodian in bankruptcy, and creating a new licence for DLT trading facilities. The first, BX Digital, received its licence in March 2025.

THE STABLECOIN LINE

Stablecoins were the most debated asset at the summit, and Switzerland's rules are among the strictest.

Under guidance issued by the regulator FINMA in July 2024, a stablecoin redeemable at par is treated as taking deposits. Its issuer needs either a banking licence or a default guarantee from a Swiss bank covering every franc owed, and must be able to identify every holder at any time.

A month after the summit, in October 2025, the Federal Council opened consultation on a reform that would create two new licences: a payment instrument institution, which would expressly allow stablecoin issuance, and a crypto institution for custody and trading. The consultation closed in February 2026. The new regime is not expected before 2028.

AI ENTERS THE FINANCIAL STACK

The other half of the summit's title was artificial intelligence.

Banks and asset managers are testing AI for research, document analysis, client service and compliance. The sessions in Zürich went further, to autonomous AI agents that can hold assets, make payments and act on a client's behalf. The organisers called this new order "Wealth³": programmable money, tokenised assets and AI agents forming the infrastructure of finance.

In finance, a mistake is more than an inconvenience. Any system that touches credit, investment, compliance or client assets needs clear boundaries, human oversight and an audit trail. Automation can speed up a process. It can speed up an error just as quickly. A session co-hosted by Citi looked further still, at what quantum computing could mean for encryption and the security of the whole stack.

The two technologies are converging. AI can help analyse transactions and flag unusual activity, while tokenised products make financial workflows programmable. Together they demand stronger security, cleaner data and tighter governance than either needs alone.

"Innovation has never been as fast as today," said Olaf Hannemann, co-founder of CV VC, "but will never be as slow ever again."

PRIVACY AND GOVERNANCE

The Swiss context brings its own demands. Financial institutions here must balance innovation with client confidentiality, cybersecurity and some of the most respected banking standards in the world.

Digital systems can make transactions more traceable and processes more automatic. They also create new risks: lost keys, software vulnerabilities and the concentration of technical control in a small number of providers. For a Swiss private bank, a token is only as trustworthy as the custody behind it.

THE INSTITUTIONAL TEST

The future of digital assets will be decided by usefulness.

Institutions adopt a technology when it settles faster, costs less, opens a market or delivers a product clients want. They hold back where the legal treatment is unclear, liquidity is thin or the operational risk is hard to control. That is why the most important sessions in Zürich were the least glamorous: integration costs, interoperability, custody standards and the resilience of networks.

Switzerland has the banks, the lawyers, the regulator and the builders within a short train ride of each other. That proximity is its real advantage.

Institutional adoption will not arrive in a single moment. It will come product by product: services that perform reliably, rules that can be followed, and businesses that can show their economics work.

The twelfth CV Summit returns in 2026.

By then, the industry will have to show that blockchain and AI have become dependable parts of financial infrastructure, and that Zürich's caution was worth the wait.
