heroes.title: F1 returns to American soil in the tech haven of Austin.
heroes.subtitle: Motorsport · After a sweltering night in Singapore, Formula 1 heads for Texas
heroes.author: Charlotte Thames

body.content:
Singapore is the race the drivers dread.

Two hours under floodlights at Marina Bay, humidity that never lifts, a street circuit of walls and kerbs that gives nothing back. In 2025 it became the first Grand Prix ever declared a Heat Hazard race under Formula 1's new rules, which meant liquid-cooled vests had to be available to every driver. Wearing one was optional. Max Verstappen chose not to.

The night belonged to George Russell. From pole position, the Mercedes driver delivered a faultless weekend and his redemption at a circuit that had broken his heart two years before.
/assets/article-f1-americas-C0U9pNN6.webp

RUSSELL'S NIGHT AT MARINA BAY

In 2023, Russell had been chasing victory in Singapore when he crashed on the final lap. In 2025 there was no such drama. He controlled the race from the front, built a ten-second cushion within 20 laps, and never let Verstappen close.

He called it payback.

Verstappen brought the Red Bull home second. Lando Norris completed the podium for McLaren, but only after a first-lap move that caused a stir: Norris dived up the inside of his teammate Oscar Piastri at Turn 1 and the two cars touched.

"That's not fair," Piastri said on the radio. McLaren chose not to order a position swap and said it would discuss the incident after the race. Norris kept it simple: "It was good racing."

MCLAREN CROWNED AGAIN

Fourth for Piastri was enough to settle the bigger prize. McLaren won the 2025 constructors' championship in Singapore, its second title in a row and the tenth in the team's history, with six races still to run. Only Red Bull in 2023 had ever clinched the title so early.

The drivers' championship is far from settled. Piastri's lead over Norris was cut to 22 points, and Verstappen, third in the standings, sits 63 points behind with the American races still to come.

THE REST OF THE FIELD

Kimi Antonelli finished fifth for Mercedes, ahead of Charles Leclerc and Fernando Alonso. Lewis Hamilton had been running fifth when his Ferrari's brakes began to fail; he dropped to seventh and then to eighth after a five-second penalty for exceeding track limits. Oliver Bearman scored for Haas in ninth, and Carlos Sainz took the final point for Williams in tenth, two weeks after his podium in Baku.

Hamilton's weekend carried more than the usual weight. He came to Singapore days after losing Roscoe, the bulldog who had been at his side, and in the paddock, for more than a decade. "It's still very painful and will be forever," he said later. The whole sport felt it with him.

THE HEAT AND THE CHAMPIONSHIP

The Heat Hazard declaration came under a new FIA rule for races where temperatures are forecast to pass 31 degrees. On the night, the air settled nearer 28 degrees, cooler than expected but still heavy with Singapore's humidity, and several drivers, Verstappen among them, raced without the cooling vests.

The physical toll is part of what makes Marina Bay special. Drivers lose kilograms of body weight over the race distance, and concentration has to hold through more than 60 laps between unforgiving walls. Russell's drive was clean from lights to flag.

The result reshaped the title fight. Norris's podium cut Piastri's lead to 22 points. Verstappen's second place kept him within reach, 63 points behind with six races left, and his form since the summer break has made McLaren look over its shoulder. With a sprint weekend in Austin offering extra points, every round from here counts double in the mind.

SINGAPORE RESULT

1 — George Russell, Mercedes
2 — Max Verstappen, Red Bull
3 — Lando Norris, McLaren
4 — Oscar Piastri, McLaren
5 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes
6 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari
7 — Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin
8 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari
9 — Oliver Bearman, Haas
10 — Carlos Sainz, Williams

NEXT STOP: AUSTIN

From one of the toughest nights of the season, Formula 1 heads to one of its biggest weekends. The United States Grand Prix runs from 17 to 19 October at the Circuit of the Americas, and it is a sprint weekend: Sprint Qualifying on Friday, the Sprint and Grand Prix qualifying on Saturday, the race on Sunday afternoon.

Austin has become something more than a race. The city's technology boom has brought money, talent and an audience that treats the weekend as a festival, and COTA leans into it. Kygo headlines the Friday night concert, Garth Brooks plays on Saturday, and Turnpike Troubadours close the weekend after the race on Sunday. In between come fan zones, simulator challenges, pit-stop competitions and enough Texas barbecue to feed the grid.

The contrast with Singapore could hardly be sharper. Marina Bay is a street circuit squeezed between buildings. COTA is a purpose-built 5.513-kilometre circuit carved into the Texas hills, with a steep climb to Turn 1 that every driver talks about, and a sequence of fast esses borrowed from the great European tracks.

THE HISTORY AT COTA

Formula 1 arrived at the Circuit of the Americas in 2012, and Hamilton won that first race for McLaren. He has made Austin his own since, winning again in 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2017 for Mercedes.

Sebastian Vettel won in 2013, Kimi Räikkönen in 2018 and Valtteri Bottas in 2019. Verstappen took three in a row from 2021 to 2023, and Leclerc won for Ferrari in 2024. Leclerc also holds the lap record, a 1:36.169 set in 2019.

That list sets up the questions for 2025. Can Verstappen reclaim a circuit he once dominated and keep his slim championship hopes alive? Can McLaren's drivers settle their rivalry on track? Can Hamilton, so often brilliant here, give Ferrari a moment to celebrate?

And there is Sainz. Williams carries the colours of the Australian software company Atlassian this season, a sponsor at home in a tech city like Austin, and after Baku the team has a taste for the podium.

THE AMERICAN CHAPTER

Formula 1's American story has changed beyond recognition. Austin, Miami and Las Vegas now give the sport three races in the United States, each with its own personality. Austin's is the most traditional and, for many fans, the most loved: a proper circuit, a passionate crowd and a city that embraces the weekend.

After Singapore's heat, Texas offers a different test. Wider spaces, faster corners, a crowd that wants a show.

The championship is still open.

Austin is waiting.

articles.title: 132nd Hurlingham Open: La Natividad La Dolfina Establish A New Standard Under Pressure
articles.excerpt: The 132nd Hurlingham Open unfolded with two teams whom are are forced to rethink their assumptions rather than rely on routine.
articles.author: Millie Sealana

body.content: The 132nd Hurlingham Open unfolded with two teams whom are are forced to rethink their assumptions rather than rely on routine. On the historic turf at Hurlingham, La Natividad La Dolfina, in their first title since the merger of the two teams, delivered a win that didn’t hinge on overpowering their opponent, but on interpreting a match that evolved in real time. It brought father and son, Adolfo and Poroto Cambiaso back on home soil.
/assets/article-cambiaso-photo1-DgZ2baVI.webp
body.caption: Photo: La Dolfina

body.content: Their 12–9 result over UAE Polo signaled far more than a strong showing at the start of the Triple Crown. It revealed a team learning to operate as a single unit, navigating momentum shifts with the kind of clarity that only comes from maturity, trust, and an unspoken internal rhythm.
/assets/article-cambiaso-photo2-BH0snRrF.webp
body.caption: Photo: La Dolfina
body.citation: Photo courtesy of Hurlingham Club / hurlinghampolo.com

body.content: A Beginning Without Clear Lines

The opening chukkers felt controlled but uncertain — not chaotic, but undefined. UAE Polo entered with a familiar structure: tight spacing, disciplined rotation, and a pace that made the early exchanges feel almost cautious. Their approach limited open lanes and challenged La Natividad La Dolfina to search for patterns rather than impose them.
Both sides tested, waited, and absorbed. The match resembled a strategic conversation where each team attempted to read the other’s intentions before revealing their own.

Camilo “Jeta” Castagnola emerged as the primary reference point. His goals — eight in total —shifting the momentum to not dip back into equilibrium. Accuracy created separation and composure controlled tempo. Bartolomé Castagnola Jr. anchored the defensive side of the equation, absorbing UAE’s heaviest attacks
Cambiaso’s Signature Influence
Adolfo Cambiaso provided the layer of interpretation needed — steering tempo, adjusting field shape, and adding the two goals that mattered more for timing than for their numbers.
Poroto Cambiaso linked the lines with fluidity, smoothing transitions from recovery to attack and ensuring the momentum held steady during the match’s most volatile periods.
Together, the four created a sense of cohesion that felt more intentional with each passing chukker.
UAE’s Challenge and the Defining Moment

UAE Polo did not retreat. They played with a controlled edge, forcing La Natividad La Dolfina into full concentration. Their strongest sequences came at moments when the match felt poised to turn — and one late collision involving Lucas Monteverde briefly froze the stadium. A penalty there could have tightened the score and reintroduced pressure. A neutral restart. Ensued.
La Natividad La Dolfina won the toss-in immediately. Momentum shifted definitively.
It was a reminder that in matches balanced this tightly, outcomes are shaped not by a single incident, but by how quickly a team can capitalize on the window it creates.
A Team Defining Itself

This victory did not lean on history or reputation. It felt like a team constructing an identity from the inside out — one built on: controlled acceleration, coordinated defensive shift and disciplined decision-making under tension
A Season Opening With Intention
With Hurlingham complete, the tour moves toward Tortugas and Palermo. La Natividad La Dolfina demonstrated their capacity to adapt, absorb pressure, and convert opportunity.
It is the kind of win that shapes a season not through spectacle, but through clarity. The road to the Triple Crown is underway. Next stop, Tortugas.

articles.title: Blazy Takes in Paris Fashion Week
articles.excerpt: Fashion · Paris · Spring/Summer 2026 · A season of debuts, and one appointment with history
articles.author: Millie Sealana

body.content:
Some fashion shows are judged as collections. Others are judged as appointments with history.

Paris Fashion Week for Spring/Summer 2026 had more of the second kind than any season in memory. Between 29 September and 7 October, the official calendar held 76 shows and 36 presentations, and running through it was a chain of debuts that redrew the map of French luxury: Jonathan Anderson's first women's collection for Dior, Pierpaolo Piccioli's first for Balenciaga, a new design duo at Loewe, Glenn Martens at Maison Margiela, Duran Lantink at Jean Paul Gaultier.

And, on Monday 6 October, the one everyone was waiting for. Matthieu Blazy's first collection for Chanel.
/assets/article-pfw-g0-QE4Mw.webp

CHANEL — A NEW ORBIT

The setting announced the ambition. The newly restored Grand Palais had become a galaxy, planets suspended in the air above a gleaming floor, as if the house were being remade from its own Big Bang.

The weight on Blazy's shoulders was considerable. Chanel had been shaped for decades by Karl Lagerfeld, who turned Gabrielle Chanel's codes into a global language, and then by Virginie Viard, who carried the house forward after Lagerfeld's death in 2019. Blazy arrived from Bottega Veneta, where his work had made luxury feel tactile rather than loud — leather that looked like denim, craft hidden in plain sight.

His first move was the boldest. For the first twenty or so looks, there was no tweed at all.

Instead came sharp tailoring, draped and layered silhouettes, unexpected colours and textures. Crisp shirting recalled the men's shirts Gabrielle Chanel borrowed and made her own. Silk gowns slid across the floor. When the tweed did arrive, it had been taken apart and rebuilt: frayed, fringed, stretched long or cut short. The bags were softened, almost crumpled, and the two-tone shoe became pliant and tactile.

CHANEL — THE MOMENT

The ending was the one nobody planned.

As Blazy came out to take his bow, to the sound of "Rhythm Is a Dancer," the model Awar Odhiang broke the runway's composure and danced towards him. The house said afterwards it had not been staged. It became the image of the week: joy, at Chanel, on the first night of a new era.

Harrods' fashion director, Simon Longland, called it his favourite debut of the season. "Outstanding," he said, singling out the shirting.

Chanel's codes are commercial assets as much as cultural symbols. The tweed suit, the chain-trimmed jacket, the two-tone shoe, the camellia, the quilted bag — customers know what they mean before they walk into a boutique. Blazy did not throw them away. He made space inside them for a new generation to recognise itself.

CHANEL — BEYOND THE RUNWAY

The stakes are higher at Chanel than almost anywhere else. It is one of the most powerful privately owned businesses in luxury, and its runway is only the visible tip. The business rests on ready-to-wear, handbags, leather goods, shoes, jewellery, watches and beauty, and a creative shift has to work across all of them, not only in photographs taken on a single evening.

Too much continuity and a house repeats itself. Too much change and it loses what customers came for. A spectacular set can frame a collection. It cannot replace one. Blazy's real test lies in what follows: how the ateliers translate his ideas, how the second and third collections build on the first, and whether customers who already know the codes find a new reason to come back.

DIOR — ANDERSON'S FIRST WOMAN

Across the city, in the Jardin des Tuileries, Jonathan Anderson presented his first women's collection for Dior, a few months after his debut menswear show for the house.

He went straight to the archive and changed it. The Bar jacket, the most famous silhouette in Dior's history, was reinterpreted. Bows and hydrangeas, two of the house's oldest motifs, appeared in new proportions. The show ended to a standing ovation.

Longland put it simply: "a revolution rather than an evolution."

For Dior, the debut closed one long chapter, Maria Grazia Chiuri's nine years at the head of womenswear, and opened another with a designer who had spent more than a decade turning Loewe into one of the most talked-about houses in fashion.

BALENCIAGA — THE HEARTBEAT

Pierpaolo Piccioli's first Balenciaga collection was called "The Heartbeat."

The salon where it was shown was scented with Getaria, the fragrance named after Cristóbal Balenciaga's home town on the Basque coast. The first look spoke directly to the founder, a clear reference to his 1957 sack dress. Piccioli also revived neo-gazar, a modern version of the stiff silk fabric Balenciaga developed in 1958.

Around those references, the collection was lighter than Balenciaga has looked in years: sculptural volumes that still moved, everyday pieces — leather jackets, chinos, T-shirts, knitwear — with altered proportions, oversized bug-eye sunglasses and elbow-length gloves. After a decade of Demna's provocations, Piccioli offered emotion and technique. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was in the audience to support him.

LOEWE — A NEW DUO

At Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, the founders of Proenza Schouler, showed their first collection on Friday 3 October.

They opened with a tribute to Ellsworth Kelly's Yellow Panel with Red Curve, then moved through a strong, almost CMYK palette that broke into mint green, coral and shocking pink. Leather, central to Loewe's identity, ran through the collection in several forms, alongside streetwear and sportswear: jeans, polos, parkas, anoraks. A new bag, the Amazona 180, was introduced.

The pair also nodded to their predecessor, revisiting the towel dress, the baby doll and the breastplate dress that defined Anderson's Loewe. It was a respectful first chapter. Their own voice will come with time.

PARIS AS THE SET

Some of the season's most striking images came from the city itself.

Celine showed in the Parc de Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, a moment of calm and intimacy in a frantic week. Saint Laurent staged its show at night against the illuminated Eiffel Tower, the kind of backdrop only Paris can offer.

Elsewhere, the debuts kept coming. Glenn Martens presented his first ready-to-wear collection for Maison Margiela. Duran Lantink took on Jean Paul Gaultier, Miguel Castro Freitas began at Mugler, and Mark Thomas at Carven.

THE POWER OF COMPRESSED ATTENTION

Fashion Week works because it concentrates the world's attention into a few days. A collection lasts minutes on the runway, then travels as photographs, reviews and social media posts, into showroom appointments and, months later, into orders. The show is theatre. Its consequences unfold over seasons.

THE OPENING, NOT THE CONCLUSION

Across the houses, buyers saw a return to elegance: lingerie details, decorative volume in feathers and fringing, black-and-white tailoring, silk scarves and bold belts. After several seasons of caution, Paris felt ready to dress up again.

But the season's real story was the change at the top. Dior, Chanel, Balenciaga and Loewe, four of the most powerful names in fashion, all opened new chapters within a single week. Their success will not be measured by one show. It will be measured in the showroom, in the boutique, and in the wardrobes of customers who have worn these houses for decades.

Blazy's first collection was the start of that conversation.

It began with a dance.

articles.author: Charlotte Thames

body.content: Pumpkins, infinity, and luminous polka worlds — Kusama's language of repetition and wonder arrives at Fondation Beyeler in Riehen, near Basel. The exhibition explores the artist's enduring fascination with the infinite, transforming the galleries into immersive environments that blur the line between viewer and artwork.
/assets/article-kusama-Kj0OfmAv.webp
body.caption: Featured image

body.content: Fondation Beyeler's setting — Renzo Piano's glass pavilion surrounded by fields and old trees — provides a contemplative counterpoint to Kusama's maximalism. The infinity rooms, the pumpkin installations, and the polka-dot trees that spill into the garden create a journey that oscillates between intimacy and overwhelm.

articles.title: Engadin Awaits the Winter
articles.excerpt: St. Moritz, the frozen lake and the season ahead
articles.author: Millie Sealana

body.content:
In late autumn, the Engadin seems to take a breath before winter. The lakes darken under a changing light, the larch forests turn gold, and the first snow settles on the high peaks.

In St. Moritz the preparations are already under way for the months that made the valley famous: racing on Corviglia, polo on the frozen lake, thoroughbreds galloping across the ice and a gathering of extraordinary cars that brings collectors to the Alps at the end of January.

The season draws people back year after year. Some come for the sport, some for the hotels and restaurants, and many because winter here has become family history. A child who first watched the horses race across the lake returns decades later with children of their own. The places change with the weather. The rituals stay.
/assets/article-engadin-Buzy8tx-.webp

THE LIGHT BEFORE THE SNOW

The Engadin runs high through the canton of Graubünden, following the Inn from the Maloja Pass towards the Lower Engadin. St. Moritz sits in the Upper Engadin, ringed by lakes and mountains that make the landscape distinctive in every season.

Autumn has its own appeal. The days shorten, the air sharpens, and the larches bring a brief wash of gold to the slopes. Walks around the lakes of Sils, Silvaplana and St. Moritz offer views that are easy to miss once the lifts are running. In the late afternoon, the peaks can turn pink and then violet as the light goes.

These quieter weeks are a good time to explore the rest of the valley. Sils, where Nietzsche spent his summers, has long drawn writers and artists. Zuoz keeps a strong sense of its historic Engadin houses, with their deep windows and sgraffito facades. The smaller villages along the valley have their own traditions, restaurants and walking routes. St. Moritz is the famous name; the Engadin's character becomes clear when a visit takes in more than one place.

For skiers, the first question is always snow, and opening dates depend on conditions and should be checked with the resorts. For everyone else, autumn is the moment to settle into the valley before the busiest weeks begin.

ST. MORITZ PREPARES FOR RACING

The Audi FIS Ski World Cup returns to St. Moritz in December, with the women's speed specialists on Corviglia. Two downhills are scheduled for Friday 12 and Saturday 13 December 2025, followed by a super-G on Sunday 14 December.

World Cup week changes the rhythm of the town. Teams, coaches, technicians and spectators arrive, and the mountain becomes a focus of international attention. This season carries extra weight: with the Milano Cortina Olympic Games in February, every downhill and super-G is also a rehearsal for the biggest stage of all.

The appeal lies in the closeness of the sport. Downhill is decided in hundredths of a second, and one line through a turn can change a result. Watching from the mountain gives a sense of the course and its terrain; following the race from town shows the people who keep the circuit running.

There is plenty to do between races. Corviglia is the heart of St. Moritz skiing, and the wider valley offers cross-country trails, winter walks and access to neighbouring ski areas. A few days are enough to combine a race day with time on the mountain and an evening in town.

POLO ON THE FROZEN LAKE

The Snow Polo World Cup returns from 23 to 25 January 2026, with six teams competing on the frozen Lake St. Moritz. Founded in 1985, it is the oldest and most important snow polo tournament in the world, and it remains one of the most recognisable fixtures of the Alpine winter.

Snow polo asks a great deal of players and horses. The surface changes the pace of the game, and the ball behaves differently from one played on grass. The setting is extraordinary: a field laid out on the lake, snow-covered mountains on every side, spectators watching from the edge of the pitch.

The tournament has a social life of its own. Friends gather for the matches, families make a weekend of it, and visitors move between the field, the town and the mountains. The audience is international, but the roots remain local, tied to the community that makes a polo field on a frozen lake possible every year.

It is a good reason to stay beyond a single match. The Engadin is at its best when the itinerary includes the landscape as well as the event: a walk before breakfast, lunch looking at the mountains, dinner in one of the valley's old stuben.

THE I.C.E.: CARS ON ICE

At the end of January the lake becomes a stage for a different kind of precision. The I.C.E. St. Moritz, the International Concours of Elegance, takes place on 30 and 31 January 2026, bringing exceptional automobiles onto the frozen lake.

Against the snow and the mountain light, the line of a classic body becomes especially clear, and details of coachwork, materials and proportion stand out in a way they rarely do in a museum hall. Friday is a static preview; on Saturday the cars move, driven on the ice in front of the crowd. Two new classes join the programme for 2026: Birth of the Hypercar, for the hybrid racers that bridged competition and the road, and Legendary Liveries, for cars remembered for their colours.

For collectors, it is a rare chance to see important cars in a setting that puts both their form and their movement at the centre. For anyone who simply loves automotive history, it gathers machines from very different eras in one remarkable place.

WHITE TURF: THE SEASON'S FINALE

February belongs to the horses. White Turf, raced on the frozen lake since 1907, returns on three Sundays — 8, 15 and 22 February 2026 — with flat races and trotting races on a course laid across the ice.

Its most famous event is unique to St. Moritz. In skikjöring, skiers are towed behind riderless thoroughbreds at speeds of up to 50 kilometres an hour around a 2,700-metre course. It looks improbable until you see it: a skier crouched low behind a galloping horse with nobody in the saddle, spray of snow, roar from the stands.

Only in St. Moritz.

THE SEASON AHEAD

From the first World Cup downhill in December to the last skikjöring race in late February, the Engadin's winter has a shape that regular visitors know by heart. Each event brings its own crowd, its own hours and its own rituals, and the valley moves from one to the next with practised ease.

What sets the place apart is how much of that winter happens outdoors, on the snow and on the ice, in a landscape that is the real host of every event. The hotels, chalets and restaurants make it comfortable. The mountains make it unforgettable.

Winter has not quite arrived.

The larches are still gold. The lakes are still water.

But the calendar is set, the first snow is on the peaks, and the Engadin is waiting.
